title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA.
METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year.
RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

title: Clinical and functional outcomes of aquatic plyometrics in adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome: a dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Optimal management of adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome requires evidence-based interventions that maximize physical recovery without overloading the patellofemoral joint. This study investigated the efficacy of aquatic plyometric (Aquatic-Plyo) exercises on pain, muscle strength, and functional disability and health-related quality of life in this demographic.
DESIGN: A dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 56 adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome (age: 10-18 years).
METHODS: Adolescents were allocated to an experimental Aquatic-Plyo group or a control group performing conventional exercises. Both arms completed 45-min sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks. Pre- and post-treatment assessments included pain intensity, isokinetic knee (quadriceps and hamstrings) torque at 120°/s and 180°/s, functional disability, and health-related quality of life.
RESULTS: Mixed-model ANOVA confirmed the therapeutic dominance of the Aquatic-Plyo protocol. It yielded superior pain relief (p = 0.004, η2p = 0.14) and larger increases in quadriceps [120°/s (p = 0.006, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.008, η2p = 0.12)] and hamstring [120°/s (p = 0.007, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09)] peak torque. Moreover, the Aquatic-Plyo intervention drove greater reduction in functional disability (p = 0.03, η2p = 0.08) and notable enhancement in perceived health-related quality of life (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09).
CONCLUSION: Aquatic-Plyo exercises effectively reduces pain and disability while improving muscle strength and health-related quality of life in adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome, making it a valuable addition to conservative rehabilitation strategies.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults.
METHODS: In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity.
RESULTS: At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

title: Platelet-Rich Plasma for Knee Osteoarthritis and Patient-Reported Outcomes: A Large Retrospective Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is used increasingly to treat knee osteoarthritis (OA). This study aimed to describe PRP use for knee OA and identify patient- and treatment-specific factors associated with clinical outcomes.
HYPOTHESIS: Patients with knee OA undergoing intra-articular PRP injections would demonstrate improvement in pain, function, and symptoms over time, with outcomes varying by patient and treatment characteristics.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: A total of 743 patients with knee OA were treated with intra-articular PRP injections. Outcomes were assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS, 0-100, higher scores indicating greater pain) and the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS-JR). Change in patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) scores from baseline and achievement of patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) were measured. Repeated-measures mixed models evaluated outcomes at baseline, 6 months, and 1 year using an all-response analysis (391 patients for Pain NRS; 400 for KOOS-JR).
RESULTS: PRP injections were associated with improvement in pain, function, and symptom state. Pain NRS improved from 39.2 at baseline to 27.2 at 6 months and 22.4 at 1 year (both P < 0.001), while KOOS-JR improved from 60.7 to 68.5 and 69.1 (both P < 0.001), with similar findings in the complete-case cohort. When stratified by radiographic severity, patients with Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grades 1 to 3 improved in both outcomes at 6 months and 1 year, while patients with KL grade 4 improved in Pain NRS at 1 year (P < 0.001) and KOOS-JR at 6 months (P = 0.01) and 1 year (P = 0.001). PASS achievement rates increased over time for both pain and function.
CONCLUSION: Intra-articular PRP injections were associated with improvements in pain, function, and symptoms in patients with knee OA. Differences between complete-case and all-response analyses suggest that follow-up patterns may influence estimated treatment response.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings describe patient-reported outcomes after intra-articular PRP injection for knee OA. Because this study lacked a control group, findings should not be interpreted as evidence that PRP caused the observed improvements.

title: The Potential Impact of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed for mood disorders. Their association with musculoskeletal side effects raises the question of potential SSRI impact on exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this prospective cohort study was to determine if SSRI use influences muscle function following a bout of eccentric exercise designed to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
METHODS: Subjects between 18 and 30 years of age were recruited in a university setting. This included 1 group taking SSRIs prescribed by their health care provider, and a control group not using SSRIs. Subjects performed a DOMS induction protocol consisting of 300 eccentric knee extensions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Muscle soreness, thigh circumference, quadriceps flexibility, and isometric quadriceps strength were measured at baseline and at 24-, 48-, 72-, and 96-hour post-DOMS protocol. Comparisons were made between SSRI users and control subjects.
RESULTS: Thirty-six subjects included 18 SSRI users and 18 controls. The DOMS protocol induced muscle soreness in both groups (P < .001 when compared with baseline). At 72 hours a between-group difference was observed for thigh muscle flexibility (MD = 11.2, SE = 5.0, 95% CI [0.9, 21.4], P = .033, ηp2 = .126) but no additional significant between-group differences in soreness, strength, thigh circumference, or flexibility were noted at any timepoint.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this population, SSRI use had no effect on muscle soreness, circumference, or strength of the quadriceps following eccentric DOMS-inducing exercise. A difference in flexibility between SSRI and control groups at a single time point likely reflects a Type 1 error and is not likely of clinical consequence. These findings suggest SSRIs do not impair short-term recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in healthy young adults, but potential SSRI impacts on longer-term training adaptations and recovery in athletic populations remain unknown.

title: Impact of total hip arthroplasty on multidimensional functioning and sleep in patients with hip osteoarthritis: A prospective cohort study.
abstract: BackgroundTotal hip arthroplasty (THA) is an established intervention for managing advanced osteoarthritis, offering substantial improvements in pain relief. However, relationship between sleep quality and functional outcomes after THA remains underexplored.ObjectiveThis longitudinal study aimed to evaluate changes in nocturnal sleep quality and daytime sleepiness and their association with functional recovery in 55 patients undergoing primary THA.MethodsPatients undergoing primary THA were enrolled in this prospective cohort study. Nocturnal sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, functional outcomes, and health-related quality of life were assessed preoperatively and at one, three, and sixxs months postoperatively using the PSQI, ESS, WOMAC, HOOS, and SF-36. Statistical analyses included Friedman's test with post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Kendall's tau correlations.ResultsWOMAC, PSQI, all HOOS dimensions, and both SF-36 components significantly improved over time. PSQI scores significantly decreased from the preoperative assessment to the postoperative follow-ups, indicating improved nocturnal sleep quality. In contrast, the median ESS score was 5 at each assessment, and no statistically significant group-level change in ESS was detected (p = 0.996). WOMAC and ESS were significantly correlated at one and six months, suggesting an association between functional recovery and daytime sleepiness at these timepoints.ConclusionsTHA was associated with significant improvements in pain, function, health-related quality of life, and nocturnal sleep quality up to six months postoperatively. No statistically significant group-level change in daytime sleepiness was detected. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, and larger prospective studies are needed to confirm them.

title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes.
METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate).
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.

title: Evolution of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: Two Decades of Evidence from the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) has evolved from a salvage procedure to a widely adopted reconstructive solution. This study performed a descriptive bibliometric and content-trend analysis of rTSA publications in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (JSES) from 2004-2025.
METHODS: A systematic review identified 506 clinical rTSA studies published in JSES between 2004 and 2025. Extracted variables included publication year, level of evidence, authorship, institution, geographic origin, research topic, demographics, indications, complications, and implant characteristics. Temporal trends were tested using Mann-Kendall trend test and segmented regression; the relationship between implant design representation and complication reporting was evaluated with Spearman rank correlation.
RESULTS: Annual publications increased significantly (BH-adjusted P < .001), peaking at 51 studies in 2023. Mean level of evidence improved (BH-adjusted P < .001), from 4.0 (2006) to 2.86 (2023). Early authorship centered on foundational surgeons (Frankle, Boileau, Walch) and European institutions, later diffusing globally. Mean age rose modestly, though this did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (BH-adjusted P = .077), stabilizing near 70-72 years after 2012. Research focus shifted from complications/technique toward outcomes after 2013, then toward instrumentation, rehabilitation, and cost. Osteoarthritis indications increased (BH-adjusted P = .005) while revision surgery declined (BH-adjusted P = .002). Implant design shifted from medialized to lateralized/non-Grammont configurations (both BH-adjusted P < .001). No individual complication subtype showed a significant temporal trend.
CONCLUSION: RTSA publication trends in JSES reflect the field's evolution from complication-focused study to evidence-driven refinement. Implant design, evidence level, and indications changed significantly, alongside, but not statistically linked to, complication reporting, informing future shoulder reconstruction research directions.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Literature Review, Bibliometric Analysis.

title: Whey Protein Isolate and Sappan Wood (Caesalpinia sappan L.) Infusion Modulates Muscle Damage and Inflammatory Biomarkers Following High-Intensity Interval Training in Sedentary Males.
abstract: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) can induce muscle damage and inflammatory responses, particularly in sedentary individuals. This study investigated the effects of whey protein isolate (WPI) combined with sappan wood (Caesalpinia sappan L.) infusion on muscle damage and inflammation following HIIT in sedentary male individuals. This double-blind randomized controlled trial included 39 sedentary males who were allocated to three groups: WPI-sappan (n=14), WPI (n=13), and control (n=12). The participants completed treadmill-based HIIT. The WPI-sappan group received 30 g of WPI combined with a sappan wood infusion prepared from 8.3 g of sappan wood powder. The WPI group received a WPI beverage, whereas the control group consumed a carbohydrate-only drink. All beverages contained 20 g of sucrose. Supplementation was administered immediately after exercise and daily for 4 d. Serum creatine kinase (CK), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), skeletal troponin I (sTnI), interleukin (IL)-6, and IL-10 concentrations were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, and 96 h post-exercise. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance. CK concentrations increased significantly after HIIT across all groups, with significant effects of time, treatment, and the time×treatment interaction (P<0.05). The WPI-sappan group demonstrated lower CK concentrations during recovery than the control group. IL-6 concentrations were significantly lower in the WPI-sappan group (P=0.024), whereas IL-10 showed a significant time×treatment interaction (P=0.010). No significant treatment effects were observed for LDH or sTnI. WPI combined with sappan wood modulated selected biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation following HIIT in sedentary males.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication.
HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff.
STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies.
RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Silent mechanical adaptation: Passive mechanical properties of ankle-surrounding tissues in individuals with unilateral chronic ankle instability.
abstract: BackgroundChronic ankle instability (CAI) is a complex condition characterized by recurring sprains.ObjectiveOur study aimed to compare the tone, stiffness, and elasticity of the periarticular muscles, Achilles tendon (AT), and plantar fascia (PF) between the affected and non-affected limbs of individuals with unilateral CAI.MethodsThe cross-sectional study included 75 volunteers aged 18 to 45 years who had been diagnosed with CAI by a physician. Ankle instability was assessed using the Identification of Functional Ankle Instability (IdFAI). Passive mechanical properties (PMP), including frequency, stiffness, and logarithmic decrement, of the tibialis anterior (TA), peroneus longus (PL), medial and lateral gastrocnemius (MGC - LGC), AT, and PF were assessed bilaterally using the MyotonPRO. PMP were compared between sides, and relationships between IdFAI scores and PMP on the affected side were examined.ResultsThe mean age was 27.46 ± 4.23 years. Logarithmic decrement and stiffness values were higher on the affected side in the TA (p = 0.011, p = 0.027), PL (p = 0.017, p = 0.031), and PF (p = 0.020, p = 0.028) compared to the non-affected side. Logarithmic decrement was also higher in the MGC (p = 0.029) and LGC (p = 0.005). No significant difference in frequency was observed for any of these structures (p > 0.05). The AT showed no significant differences in frequency, stiffness, or logarithmic decrement between the affected and non-affected sides (p > 0.05).ConclusionsCAI is a multidimensional pathology characterized by deterioration of the PMP of the surrounding muscles and PF. These findings suggest that management of CAI should include interventions aimed at improving myofascial tissue elasticity in addition to neuromuscular rehabilitation.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, TRN: NCT06987435.

title: Differential Splinting After Zone II Flexor Tendon Repair: The Bidirectional Splint.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Zone II flexor tendon injuries remain challenging because of the risks of rupture, adhesions, and stiffness. Splint design may influence repair-site tension during early healing. We describe a novel bidirectional splint (B-splint) that applies differential tensioning and compare its outcomes with those of conventional dorsal blocking splinting.
METHODS: We retrospectively studied 59 patients (99 repaired tendons): 20 patients (31 tendons) treated with the B-splint after flexor digitorum profundus repair and 39 patients (68 tendons) treated with a dorsal blocking splint. The B-splint positions repaired digits in metacarpophalangeal flexion with interphalangeal extension while maintaining the noninjured digits in full extension. Functional outcomes were assessed using the modified Strickland score; tendon rupture and tenolysis were recorded. Categorical outcomes were compared using exact tests.
RESULTS: No ruptures occurred in the B-splint cohort versus 1 in the control cohort. Excellent outcomes occurred in 19 of 20 B-splint patients (95%) versus 30 of 39 controls (77%), favoring the B-splint without statistical significance (P = 0.141). Tenolysis was less frequent with the B-splint (5% versus 13%). No B-splint patients developed stiffness of the noninjured digits.
CONCLUSIONS: The B-splint was associated with favorable functional outcomes, no observed ruptures, and less tenolysis than conventional dorsal blocking splinting. It complements established rehabilitation strategies. Prospective studies are warranted to define its biomechanical and clinical role.

title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
abstract: Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.

title: Biomechanical comparison of parallel versus convergent screw fixation in Zadek osteotomy.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Zadek osteotomy is an increasingly utilized treatment for insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT), although an optimal fixation strategy remains unclear. This cadaveric study compared biomechanical outcomes of parallel and convergent screw fixation constructs following Zadek osteotomy. We hypothesized that convergent screw fixation would demonstrate greater stability.
METHODS: Five paired fresh-frozen human calcanei (10 specimens) underwent simulated Zadek osteotomy, receiving paired parallel and convergent screw fixations on contralateral limbs. Specimens were tested using a servohydraulic system and motion tracking. Axial loading was applied until construct failure. Primary biomechanical outcomes included construct stiffness, load at 2 mm displacement, ultimate load to failure, and displacement at failure. Comparisons were performed using paired t-tests. One specimen was excluded from final analysis due to premature failure.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed between parallel and convergent constructs for any biomechanical outcome. Mean stiffness was 1415 ± 1337 N/mm for parallel constructs and 1360 ± 952 N/mm for convergent constructs (p = 0.96). Load at 2 mm displacement measured 707 ± 289 N and 892 ± 401 N, respectively (p = 0.54). Ultimate load to failure was 915 ± 266 N and 1065 ± 401 N, respectively (p = 0.55). Displacement at failure was similar between groups (p = 0.45). The combination shear-compression sliding at the osteotomy interface was the predominant mechanism of failure in both groups.
CONCLUSION: Parallel and convergent screw constructs demonstrated comparable initial fixation strengths following Zadek osteotomy, suggesting screw trajectory may have limited impact on construct stability. Further studies are needed to validate these findings clinically.

title: Long-Term Failure Rate of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using All-Inside 4-Stranded Semitendinosus Autograft Is 20.5.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate outcomes (graft failure, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures, and knee stability) after primary isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using the all-inside technique with 4-stranded semitendinosus autograft fixed between 2 adjustable-loop cortical suspension devices, with a minimum follow-up of 10 years.
METHODS: Patients who underwent primary isolated ACL reconstruction using the all-inside 4-stranded semitendinosus between January 2011 and January 2013, with a minimum of 10-year follow-up, were included. Patients completed a standardized questionnaire and were offered a follow-up consultation. The questionnaire included the Tegner, ACL-Return to Sport after Injury, Subjective Knee Value, subjective International Knee Documentation Committee, and assessment of graft failure. Clinical evaluations and laxity measurements were conducted during follow-up consultations.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 138 months (range: 122-159), 156 patients completed the questionnaire, and 111 were clinically evaluated. The mean age was 39.6 ± 9.7 years (range: 15-62). Graft failure occurred in 20.5% of cases (32/156). The mean decrease in Tegner was 1.03 ± 1.23 points, and 51% returned to their preinjury sport level. The median preoperative Tegner was 7.0 (interquartile range: 6.0-7.0). A higher preoperative Tegner was associated with an increased risk of graft failure (P = .016). Graft failure occurred in 23% of males and 16.6% of females (P = .461). Patients with grafts sized ≤8 mm (n = 85) had a failure rate of 17.5%, compared with 23.9% for grafts >8 mm (P = .441). The mean subjective International Knee Documentation Committee was 85.6 ± 13.5, Subjective Knee Value 79.2 ± 22.1, and ACL-Return to Sport after Injury 69.5 ± 26.5. Among patients without reported graft failure, 16.5% exhibited >3 mm differential anterior laxity, and 28% had a pivot-shift score ≥2.
CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 10-year follow-up, primary isolated ACL reconstruction using an all-inside 4-stranded semitendinosus autograft showed a 20.5% graft failure rate, despite favorable patient-reported outcomes. A higher preoperative Tegner showed a trend toward increased graft failure.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Low Artificial Intelligence-Estimated Bone Mineral Density From Chest Radiographs Is Associated With Delayed Pain Recovery and Lower Quality of Life After Medial Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Whether bone quality influences recovery after medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) remains uncertain, partly because bone mineral density (BMD) is not routinely evaluated using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry before UKA. This study investigated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-estimated proximal femur BMD derived from preoperative chest radiographs was associated with longitudinal patient-reported outcomes after cemented medial UKA.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 342 consecutive cemented medial UKAs performed from 2012 to 2023. After exclusions, 336 procedures were categorized according to AI-estimated proximal femur young adult mean (YAM), with low estimated BMD defined as YAM less than 80%. Propensity-score matching based on age, sex, body mass index, and diagnosis identified 58 low-BMD procedures and 58 matched controls. Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) subscales were evaluated preoperatively and up to three years postoperatively. Linear mixed-effects models assessed group-by-time interactions.
RESULTS: After matching, baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Both groups demonstrated postoperative improvement across all KOOS subscales. Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for KOOS pain (P < 0.001) and quality of life (QOL) (P = 0.010), whereas no significant interactions were identified for symptoms, activities of daily living, or sport/recreation. The low BMD group had lower pain scores at three months, six months, and one year, as well as lower QOL scores at one, two, and three years. The one-year postoperative range of motion, alignment, component positioning, and radiographic migration or subsidence did not significantly differ between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Low AI-estimated proximal femur BMD from routine chest radiographs was associated with delayed early pain recovery and statistically lower knee-related QOL from one to three years after cemented medial UKA. Opportunistic AI-based BMD screening may identify candidates for preoperative bone health evaluation and counseling.

title: Five-Year Outcomes and Return to Sport After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in Young Patients With Minimal (<10%) or No Glenoid Bone Loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Arthroscopic Bankart repair is commonly used to address anterior instability in adolescents and young adults with no or minimal bone loss. However, failure rates remain high, particularly in high-risk populations.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate clinical outcomes, return-to-sport (RTS) rates, and predictors of failure after arthroscopic Bankart repair in patients ≤24 years of age with minimal glenoid bone loss. It was hypothesized that patients would demonstrate favorable outcomes, low recurrence rates, and high RTS rates, and smaller distance-to-dislocation (DTD) measurements, and contact sports participation would be associated with failure.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: The data of patients with anterior shoulder instability and minimal bone loss (<10%) who underwent primary arthroscopic Bankart repair between 2006 and 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. Remplissage was not performed. Data collected included preoperative instability events, patient-reported outcome measures, satisfaction, radiographic measurements (glenoid bone loss, glenoid track, and DTD), and RTS outcomes. Failure was defined as re-dislocation or recurrent instability requiring surgery.
RESULTS: A total of 130 patients were evaluated; 18 were excluded, leaving 112. Of these, 96 patients (85.7%) were available for the final follow-up (mean age, 19.9 ± 3.1 years; mean follow-up, 68.4 ± 42.7 months). All clinical outcomes improved significantly (P < .05) except for the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey Mental Component Summary score. The median satisfaction score was 9 (IQR, 8-10). Participation in contact sports was associated with failure, while other risk factors were not. RTS was achieved by 96.1% of patients; however, only 57.1% returned to their preinjury level. Fewer preoperative dislocation events were associated with successful return to full activity (P = .04). The recurrence rate was 33.3%, and revision surgery was required in 19 patients (19.8%).
CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic Bankart repair was associated with high rates of recurrence and revision surgery in a series of patients ≤24 years of age without glenoid bone loss. In those who did not require revision surgery, clinical outcomes and RTS rates were high. Contact sports participation was associated with failure. A greater number of preoperative instability events negatively influence RTS outcomes. Arthroscopic Bankart repair in this population is safe and has a low complication rate, but the failure rate remains considerable.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.

title: Validity of triaxial accelerometer for estimating total energy expenditure in elite female university athletes: a doubly labeled water study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Accurate estimation of total energy expenditure (TEE) in athletes is essential for determining energy requirements to support training, recovery, and performance. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is one of the key components associated with the accuracy of TEE estimation. However, few studies have evaluated the accuracy of BMR and TEE estimation methods in athletic populations.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to examine the validity of the Cunningham equation for BMR estimation and the accelerometer-based method (ACCTRI) for TEE estimation in elite female university runners, using the doubly labeled water (DLW) method as the reference criterion.
METHODS: We analyzed data from 16 elite female university runners (mean age 20 ± 1 years). We assessed: (1) the association and agreement between BMR estimated using the Cunningham equation and BMR measured by indirect calorimetry, and (2) the association and agreement between TEE estimated using the ACCTRI method and TEE measured using the DLW method.
RESULTS: Correlational analysis revealed significant, positive, and strong associations between estimated and measured BMR (r = 0.728, P = 0.001) and between estimated and measured TEE (r = 0.828, P = 0.001). Bland-Altman analyses showed good agreement between estimated and measured BMR (bias, ~1.6%). The mean TEE difference between two method was 416 ± 242 kcal/day.
CONCLUSIONS: The Cunningham equation provides reasonably accurate estimates of BMR. ACCTRI overestimated TEE by approximately 12% compared to DLW, thus support staff should consider this when supporting female runners.

title: Structured Physiotherapy Improves Functional Outcomes in Acromegalic Arthropathy After Biochemical Remission: A Prospective Controlled Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal symptoms frequently persist in acromegaly despite biochemical remission, yet the impact of structured physiotherapy on pain, stiffness, and function remains poorly defined.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a standardized knee-focused physiotherapy program in controlled acromegaly and to identify clinical predictors of treatment responsiveness.
METHODS: Thirteen patients with acromegaly in remission and 13 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched individuals with primary knee osteoarthritis completed a 15-session physiotherapy program. Outcomes were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and WOMAC. Minimal clinically significant difference (MCID) thresholds (≥2 for BPI, ≥10 for WOMAC) determined meaningful improvement. Correlation analyses examined associations between clinical variables and Δ scores.
RESULTS: Acromegaly patients showed significant improvements in all BPI and WOMAC domains (p<0.001). MCID was achieved by 85% for BPI and 100% for WOMAC Total. Pain and function improved most, whereas stiffness showed limited responsiveness. Compared with osteoarthritis controls, acromegaly patients demonstrated smaller Δ changes; baseline-adjusted analyses (ANCOVA) indicated that this attenuated response was largely explained by greater baseline severity in the control group, whereas the persistently greater stiffness in acromegaly remained significant even after adjustment. BMI correlated positively with improvements in BPI Total (r = 0.63) and BPI Pain Severity (r = 0.69), while adenoma size correlated negatively with both measures (r = -0.57 and -0.60). BMI showed a negative association with WOMAC Total improvement (r = -0.59). Stiffness changes were strongly negatively correlated with pretreatment IGF-1 (r = -0.77).
CONCLUSION: Structured physiotherapy yields clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function in acromegaly, while stiffness appears less reversible and more structurally driven. Early musculoskeletal assessment and physiotherapy integration may enhance long-term management.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

title: Talking about menstruation in professional women's sport: gendered communication between athletes, coaches and team-mates.
abstract: Communication about menstruation remains uneven within sporting environments despite growing recognition of the importance of menstrual health for athletes. This article investigates how female athletes communicate about menstruation and how gendered hierarchies shape these interactions. The analysis is based on responses to an online questionnaire completed by Polish professional athletes (N = 253). The findings indicate that menstruation is seldom discussed between athletes and coaches, with participants identifying social and institutional barriers, including menstrual taboo and the predominance of male coaches. In contrast, athletes reported discussing menstruation more openly with female team-mates, where such conversations often facilitated mutual support and the sharing of experiential knowledge about menstrual health. These interactions suggest that women's teams can function as 'counterspaces' where menstrual experiences can be acknowledged and normalised in ways largely absent from coach-athlete relationships. Findings highlight the importance of creating environments in which menstrual health can be openly discussed, as limited communication about menstruation may restrict athletes' access to information, support, and health-related guidance. By examining menstruation as a topic of health-related communication, the study contributes to scholarship on gender, embodiment and menstrual health, highlighting how institutional hierarchies shape the visibility and discussion of bodily processes across different social contexts.

title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

title: A two-factor framework to assess international male field hockey movement characteristics: Implications for performance preparation.
abstract: We aimed to establish the nature and structure of the relationships between high-intensity movement characteristics during international field hockey matches. Global positioning system data were obtained from 28 elite male field hockey players (n = 393 international player-matches). Mean and 90% trimmed range were extracted for the 10 most intense 1-min periods (separated by >60s) for: total distance (m); high-speed distance (>5 m·s-1); sprint distance (>7 m·s-1); accelerations (>2.5 m·s-2); decelerations (<-2.5 m·s-2) and high-speed cuts (>45° change-of-direction at >5 m·s-1). Pearson's correlations were calculated for pairs of characteristics (summed across the 10 most intense periods). An exploratory factor analysis was then applied to movement characteristics. Finally, factors were validated by testing whether they discriminated between playing positions using random-effect linear-mixed models. Factor analysis explained 76% of total variance (χ42 = 286, p < 0.001) and resulted in a two-factor solution: 'Distance' (total, high-speed and sprint distance), and 'Acceleration' (accelerations and decelerations). High-speed cuts loaded onto both factors. The two factors also discriminated significantly between playing positions. Our data-driven approach indicates that Distance and Acceleration are distinct factors of international male field hockey, specifically, Midfielders cover more distance than Defenders, and Strikers change speed and direction more than Midfielders or Defenders. Practitioners should consider prescribing and monitoring these distinct factors separately.

title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

title: Multidimensional Pre-Competition Stress Profiles in Wheelchair Basketball: Associations with Cortisol and Psychological Indicators.
abstract: This study examined pre-competition cortisol levels and psychological anticipation in wheelchair basketball athletes using a person-centred approach. Thirty-four male athletes (mean age: 35 ± 7.75 years) competing in a regional league provided saliva samples 35-50 min before competition and completed psychological assessments with the Revised Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2R) and the Perceived Stress Scale. K-Means cluster analysis (k = 3), validated by Ward's hierarchical clustering (ARI = 0.947; NMI = 0.892) and Bootstrap Jaccard stability (0.544-0.603), identified three exploratory stress profiles: Low Reactor (n = 5; low cortisol, anxiety, and stress), High Reactor (n = 20; moderate cortisol, high cognitive/physical anxiety), and Physiological Stress Reactor (n = 9; high cortisol, high stress, moderate anxiety). Significant group differences were observed for log(Cortisol) (H(2) = 17.095, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.518), Cognitive Anxiety (H(2) = 13.900, p < 0.01, ε2 = 0.421), Somatic Anxiety (H(2) = 18.840, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.571), and Perceived Stress (H(2) = 21.831, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.662), while self-confidence did not differ. Exploratory logistic regression indicated that functional classification, years of sport participation, match location, and match result did not significantly predict the Physiological Stress Reactor membership. These findings suggest that pre-competition stress-related characteristics may manifest in different combinations of physiological and psychological indicators. The identified profiles should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger and independent samples.

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Delayed return to sport after fat pad debridement: A surgical effect or a load-tolerance signal?
abstract: This Letter responds to the meta‑analysis entitled 'Fat pad debridement prolongs return-to-sport: A meta-analysis and meta-regression of surgical interventions for chronic patellar tendinopathy' by Jolly et al., which examined surgical interventions for chronic patellar tendinopathy. We contend that the observed delay should not be attributed solely to the surgical procedure. Fat pad debridement may serve as a marker of a more irritable anterior-knee pain phenotype, given that fat pad pathology frequently coexists with impingement, fibrosis and peritendinous irritation. Furthermore, time to return to sport (RTS) is an incomplete recovery surrogate; meaningful restoration depends on rebuilding tendon load tolerance rather than meeting a single chronological milestone. We therefore advise interpreting the association as a composite signal of procedural, phenotypic and rehabilitative factors. Future prospective studies should document preoperative fat pad status, extent of debridement and criterion-based RTS progression, so as to determine whether fat pad preservation truly accelerates recovery or whether delayed RTS simply identifies athletes needing more individualized load management.

title: Conservative Management of a Displaced Iliopsoas Avulsion in an Adolescent: A Case Report and Systematic Review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To report a case of traumatic iliopsoas tendon avulsion with displacement exceeding the commonly cited 2-cm surgical threshold, managed successfully without surgery, and to systematically review the literature on optimal treatment and return-to-sport outcomes.
DESIGN: Case report combined with a PRISMA-compliant systematic review of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Embase.
SETTING: Level I university trauma center; systematic review of published case reports and series.
PARTICIPANTS: A 16-year-old male competitive soccer player (index case) and 58 additional patients from the literature, predominantly adolescent males with sports-related iliopsoas avulsion.
INTERVENTIONS: The index patient received conservative treatment with staged weight bearing and structured physiotherapy. Across the literature, 90% (52/58) were treated conservatively and 10% operatively.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Clinical recovery, strength restoration, radiographic union on MRI, and return to sport.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies (58 patients; 59 including this case) were analyzed. A bony lesser-trochanter avulsion was present in 98% (57/58). Of at least 9 patients with displacement >2 cm, 5 recovered fully nonoperatively. The index patient was pain-free with full strength and unrestricted soccer return at 3 months; 6-month MRI showed radiographic nonunion despite complete functional recovery. Return to sport approached 100%, typically within 10 to 12 weeks.
CONCLUSIONS: Available very low-certainty evidence suggests that nonoperative management can achieve favorable clinical recovery and return to sport after traumatic iliopsoas avulsion, including in some cases with displacement greater than 2 cm. Return-to-sport decisions may reasonably prioritize restored, pain-free function over radiographic union, but larger prospective studies are needed.

title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS: Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade.
RESULTS: Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density.
CONCLUSIONS: Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.

title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists.
METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress.
CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.
