title: Discussing pain increases at the point of exercise prescription: a clinical commentary for persistent musculoskeletal conditions.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with persistent musculoskeletal pain frequently perform prescribed exercise without direct supervision. When exercise increases symptoms, patients may be uncertain whether to continue, modify the session, or seek advice. A prescription that specifies exercises and dosage but provides no guidance about possible symptom aggravation may therefore leave an important gap in preparation.
PURPOSE: This commentary proposes that, when prescribed exercise may increase pain, the possible response should be discussed at the point of prescription and that clinicians should prepare patients for how symptom aggravation will be interpreted and reviewed.
DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS: Trials comparing painful and nonpainful exercise, including an updated 2025 systematic review, show no consistent advantage for either approach and provide no basis for a universal adjustment rule. Pain-monitoring protocols developed for Achilles tendinopathy indicate that continued loading can be compatible with recovery in that condition, but their thresholds have not been validated for other presentations and should not be transferred by default. Features of altered nociceptive processing may further complicate interpretation of symptom aggravation but do not remove the need for assessment. What is proposed is a conversation rather than an algorithm: an explicit discussion, established when exercise is prescribed, about what a symptom increase might mean, how it will be interpreted, and when and how the plan will be reviewed. The evidence considered spans low back pain, osteoarthritis, and tendinopathy; extension to other persistent musculoskeletal conditions remains a reasonable but untested proposition.
CONCLUSION: Research should establish what instructions clinicians currently provide when exercise increases pain, whether patients understand them, and which responses lead patients to continue, modify, or abandon exercise. Future studies should also determine whether discussing possible aggravation before it occurs improves adherence, confidence, function, and timely reassessment.

title: Noninvasive assessment of the anaerobic threshold in endurance athletes: an evidence-based narrative review of methods, validity, and field feasibility.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION OR BACKGROUND: The anaerobic threshold (AnT) marks the transition between heavy and severe exercise intensity domains and guides training prescription and performance monitoring. Criterion methods (blood lactate and gas exchange) are accurate but invasive, costly, or impractical outside laboratories, prompting the search for noninvasive surrogates. This review evaluates the validity of these estimation procedures rather than the underlying physiology.
SOURCES OF DATA: MEDLINE (via PubMed) was searched from inception without language restrictions, supplemented by reference-list and citation searching. Eligible studies compared noninvasive AnT indices, including heart rate variability (HRV; including detrended fluctuation analysis [DFA] α1), cardiac repolarization instability, heart rate deflection/field slope-variation methods, critical power (CP)/ critical speed (CS), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), the talk test, and machine-learning (ML) models, with criterion standards. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Eighty-eight reports were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed.
AREAS OF AGREEMENT: DFA α1, NIRS breakpoints, and CP/CS show strong associations with laboratory criteria and increasing field applicability through wearables. Accuracy and feasibility trade-offs require method selection according to the threshold, sport, and required precision.
AREAS OF CONTROVERSY: Correlation indicates group-level association rather than individual agreement; Bland-Altman and reliability analyses are more informative for substitution. Criterion standards are not interchangeable, and heart rate deflection is not consistently identifiable. Evidence in female athletes remains limited.
GROWING POINTS: Multimodal wearables integrating HRV, muscle oxygenation, and running power with ML may improve field-based threshold estimation.
AREAS FOR DEVELOPING RESEARCH: Priorities include standardized reporting, transparent bias assessment, female-athlete validation, and broader systematic and meta-analytic synthesis.

title: The content and reporting completeness of physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis: a systematic review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study synthesised the content and reporting completeness of published physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis (GHOA).
METHODS: This systematic review undertook electronic database searches in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane, CINAHL and PEDro (until June 2025) for any peer-reviewed articles/studies describing physical therapist-led interventions across non-surgical and perioperative settings for adults aged 45 years and over with GHOA. The content and reporting completeness were synthesized using the 22-item Template for Intervention Description and Replication for rehabilitation interventions (TIDIeR_Rehab).
RESULTS: Overall, 134 articles/studies describing 156 physical therapist-led interventions were included, comprising mostly case series designs (n=47, 35.1%) or narrative reviews (n=38, 28.4%). Of the remaining 49 articles/studies, only 11 were studies reporting RCT results and three were protocols of RCTs in progress. Intervention content varied considerably, and the overall completeness of intervention item reporting was poor (only 18%). Interventions in non-surgical contexts commonly included strengthening exercises (n=33, 53.2%), range of motion (ROM) exercises (n=23, 37.1%), and electrotherapy modalities (n=16, 25.8%). Sling immobilisation was most reported in postoperative interventions (n=64, 72.7%). Many different proposed mechanisms of action were reported (n=49, 31.4%); but all were biomechanically orientated.
CONCLUSION: Very few high-quality empirical studies evaluating physical therapist-led interventions for GHOA have been published. We found substantial heterogeneity in the content of published physical therapist-led interventions, and the reporting completeness was generally poor. This suggests considerable uncertainty regarding best practice physical therapy for GHOA in terms of intervention content. Future high-quality empirical research is needed, preferably using RCT designs that include clear descriptions of interventions.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Effects of Integrative Neuromuscular Training on Unilateral and Bilateral Lower-Extremity Sports Performance in Adolescent Female Sprinters: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent female athletes often exhibit more pronounced lower-limb asymmetry due to physiological differences, increasing injury risk. Despite documented efficacy in team sports for injury mitigation and performance enhancement, integrative neuromuscular training (INT) effects on unilateral and bilateral lower-limb capabilities in trained adolescent female sprinters remain undetermined.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that an 8-week INT program would significantly improve unilateral and bilateral lower-extremity performance measures in adolescent female sprinters compared with traditional sprint-specific training.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Twenty-four national second-level adolescent female sprinters (aged 16-18 years) were randomly assigned to an 8-week INT group (n = 12) or a control group (CON, n = 12) that continued traditional sprint-specific training. Measurements obtained before and after the intervention included the hop test, star excursion balance test (SEBT), 3-repetition maximum (3RM) unilateral and bilateral back squat, 100-m run, standing long jump (SLJ), and limb symmetry index (LSI).
RESULTS: After the intervention, the INT group outperformed the CON group on the nondominant side in all hop tests (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.74-0.88), six directions of the SEBT (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.44-0.88), and the 3RM unilateral back squat (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.65). On the dominant side, the INT group also outperformed the CON group in the single hop for distance (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.80) and three directions of the SEBT (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.38-0.84). In addition, the INT group showed significantly greater improvements than the CON group in the LSI from unilateral tests (all P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.26-0.88), as well as in the 100-m run and SLJ (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.61-0.69).
CONCLUSION: The 8-week INT program was associated with improvements in dynamic balance, explosive power, and limb symmetry in adolescent female sprinters, with greater benefits observed on the nondominant side.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: INT is an effective training modality for improving lower-limb performance and mitigating asymmetry in adolescent female sprinters.

title: Creatine supplementation in soccer players: a systematic review.
abstract:
AIM: Soccer places repeated demands on short-duration, high-intensity performance, including sprints, accelerations, jumps, and technical actions performed over the course of a match. Because these efforts depend heavily on rapid adenosine triphosphate (ATP) resynthesis, creatine is a plausible ergogenic aid for soccer players. However, findings in soccer-specific studies have been inconsistent, and previous reviews have addressed narrower questions using smaller evidence sets. This systematic review therefore examined the effects of creatine supplementation on performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes in soccer players.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 15 May 2025 in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. We included controlled clinical trials of creatine supplementation in male or female soccer players of any age or competitive level when an eligible placebo, control, or comparison condition was available. Outcomes were grouped into performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue domains. Domains from the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2) and the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool were used to produce study-level methodological summaries rather than formal result-specific risk-of-bias assessments. Because the studies differed substantially in design, supplementation protocols, populations, and outcomes, findings were synthesised qualitatively rather than pooled in a meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Source-level verification left 45 eligible reports representing 41 unique studies: 28 randomised parallel-group studies, 2 randomised crossover/repeated-condition studies, and 11 non-randomised or allocation-unverifiable controlled studies. Some trials reported favourable findings for repeated-sprint performance, anaerobic power, and muscular strength, but the comparative evidence was inconsistent and the certainty of evidence was very low. Findings for vertical jump performance and technical skills were mixed, while change-of-direction and endurance outcomes showed no consistent benefit. Recovery- and fatigue-related findings were also largely null or inconsistent. Body mass often increased, particularly after loading protocols, whereas evidence for gains in lean mass was limited and inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: The soccer-specific evidence for creatine supplementation remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Favourable findings have been reported for some repeated-sprint, anaerobic-power, and strength outcomes, but the comparative evidence is heterogeneous, often limited by unclear or nonsignificant between-group effects, and of very low certainty. Firm conclusions about efficacy are therefore not possible. Body mass commonly increased, especially after loading protocols, while effects on lean mass, endurance, change-of-direction ability, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Predicting Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Injury in National Football League Players Using Machine Learning.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: BackgroundNational Football League (NFL) players frequently experience Achilles tendon (AT) injuries. However, there is mixed evidence regarding factors influencing return to play (RTP) after AT injury. The objective of this study is to develop machine learning models to predict NFL players' likelihood of RTP within 1 year of an AT tear.
HYPOTHESIS: Machine learning models can predict 1-year RTP status in NFL players following AT tear.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective Cohort.MethodsA retrospective review was conducted to identify NFL players who sustained unilateral AT injuries from 2004 to 2024. Player demographics and performance data were recorded. Return to play was defined as generating playing statistics. Five machine learning models were developed: logistic regression, random forest classifier, XGBoost, Gaussian naive Bayes, and K-nearest neighbors. Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 were used to assess model performance.ResultsOne hundred seventy-six NFL players were identified with an AT injury. One hundred eight players achieved RTP within 1 year (class 1), while 63 players did not (class 0). In the full cohort, injury etiology was the most influential feature associated with 1-year RTP, followed by pre-injury performance. Among the 99 players with a confirmed AT tear, 48 players achieved RTP within 1 year (class 1), while 51 players did not (class 0). Within the confirmed-tear cohort, draft round and games started were the leading predictors of 1-year RTP, which was best predicted by random forest with a mean accuracy of 0.69, precision of 0.68, recall of 0.70, and an F1-score of 0.69 for class 0.ConclusionMachine learning models that combine clinical and performance metrics of NFL athletes demonstrated potential for predicting 1-year RTP after AT injury and identifying factors associated with RTP.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Machine learning could be integrated into clinical decision-making and prognosis to refine rehabilitation approaches in NFL players.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.

title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years.
OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation.
RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate.
CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

title: Muscle biomechanical rehabilitation following therapy in Achilles and patellar tendinopathy assessed by MR elastography.
abstract: Tendon healing is the primary goal of tendinopathy therapy. However, the therapeutic response of adjacent muscles remains uninvestigated. MR-elastography (MRE) can assess muscle biomechanical properties and function. This study investigated muscle biomechanical responses in patients treated for patellar (PT) or Achilles tendinopathy (AT). A prospective longitudinal study included 20 athletes, 8 with AT (41 years ± 8; 6 men) and 12 with PT (34 years ± 10; 12 men), who underwent MRI, diffusion-tensor-imaging (DTI), and MRE before and ≥6 months post-treatment. Isotropic (ciso) and anisotropic stiffness parameters (c‖ and c⊥) in tendon-adjacent muscles were derived and analyzed between groups and longitudinally compared with clinical scores and tendon dimensions. At baseline, symptomatic legs with higher tendon dimensions and clinical symptoms exhibited lower muscle stiffness than asymptomatic legs (p<0.05). Post-treatment, AT patients showed increased ciso (4.3±8.5%) in gastrocnemius and posterior soleus (SolP; 4.9±8.6%) in treated legs but decreased SolP stiffness (-3.2±7.2%) in untreated legs (p<0.05). In PT patients, only anisotropic MRE (c‖: 5.3±15.2% and c⊥: 10.3±12.7%) in vastus lateralis showed significant increases (p<0.05) post-treatment. In treated legs of AT and PT, increased muscle stiffness post-treatment correlated negatively with tendon dimensions (p<0.05). Post-therapy, tendon-adjacent muscles exhibited increased stiffness in affected leg and decreased stiffness in contralateral leg (particularly SolP), potentially reflecting altered muscle use and loading, respectively. The observed changes in muscle stiffness may help characterize muscle biomechanical changes during rehabilitation and balanced recovery. Furthermore, anisotropic muscle stiffness was more sensitive to tendon structural changes than isotropic stiffness, warranting further validation for clinical assessment.

title: [Disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders among athletes II.].
abstract: Over the past two and a half decades, a substantial shift has occurred in the understanding of disordered eating and eating disorders among athletes. Research has gradually moved beyond the concept of the female athlete triad towards the model of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), which recognizes low energy availability as a key factor affecting both athletes' health and performance. The aim of this study is to review the international literature published between 2000 and 2025 on disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes, with particular emphasis on prevalence, the contemporary interpretation of risk factors, the development of the REDs concept, and current recommendations for screening, treatment, and prevention. A thematic narrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases. Publications and professional consensus statements addressing disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency, screening, prevention, and multidisciplinary care in athletes were included in the analysis. The reviewed literature indicates that disordered eating behaviors are considerably more prevalent than clinically diagnosed eating disorders; however, both conditions adversely affect athletes' health and performance. The evidence also confirms that low energy availability is not exclusively associated with eating disorders but may also result from an imbalance between energy intake and exercise expenditure. The introduction of the REDs model substantially expanded the earlier female athlete triad concept by highlighting the involvement of male athletes, the role of psychological factors, and the multisystem consequences of low energy availability. Current international recommendations emphasize early identification, sport-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care as the cornerstones of effective prevention and treatment. Contemporary approaches to nutrition-related problems in athletes consider disordered eating, eating disorders, and relative energy deficiency as interrelated conditions. The development of standardized multidisciplinary models of care consistent with current international recommendations would be warranted in Hungary. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1702-1709.

title: Short-term effects of extracorporeal shockwave therapy and low-level laser therapy on clinical outcomes and ultrasonographic tendon thickness in lateral elbow tendinopathy.
abstract: BackgroundThis study aimed to compare the short-term effects of extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) on pain, elbow function, health-related quality of life, hand grip strength, and ultrasonographic extensor tendon thickness in patients with LET.ObjectiveIn this prospective, randomized, controlled, single-blind trial, patients with LET were randomly assigned to either ESWT or LLLT. Both groups received the same standardized home exercise program and lateral epicondylitis brace. Visual Analog Scale (VAS), the Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE), Short Form-36 (SF-36), hand grip strength, and ultrasonographic evaluation were assessed before and after three weeks of randomisation.ResultsAt three weeks, the ESWT group demonstrated significantly lower post-treatment pain intensity (VAS) than the LLLT group (p = 0.004). ESWT was also associated with significantly better outcomes in PRTEE pain scores (p = 0.030), ultrasonographic tendon thickness (p = 0.021), and the Role Physical (p = 0.029) and General Health (p = 0.005) domains of the SF-36. No significant between-group differences were observed in hand grip strength, PRTEE function, PRTEE total score, or the remaining SF-36 domains.ConclusionWhen used as adjuncts to a standardized exercise program and LET brace, ESWT was associated with greater short-term pain reduction and more favorable outcomes in the PRTEE pain subscale, ultrasonographic tendon thickness, and selected domains of health-related quality of life compared with LLLT. These findings suggest that ESWT may offer greater short-term pain-related benefits than LLLT when both are added to exercise and bracing.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Early sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing characteristics and six-month knee extensor strength after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether quadriceps motor unit firing rates measured pre-operatively and during the first three months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction are associated with isometric knee extensor strength at six months, and to explore the relationship between motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude and firing rate.
METHODS: Twenty-seven participants (15 female) underwent surface electromyography of vastus medialis and vastus lateralis during sub-maximal isometric knee extension from pre-operation to three months post-reconstruction. Six-month knee extensor MVC force was modelled using Bayesian regression and interpreted using a region of practical equivalence (ROPE; ±15 N). A secondary hierarchical analysis examined MUAP amplitude and firing rate.
RESULTS: Motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with six-month knee extensor strength across time points and limbs. In the ACL reconstructed limb at two weeks, a 1-SD greater mean firing rate was associated with 45.8 N greater six-month strength (95% credible interval [CrI] - 18.5 to 114.6 N). Six-month strength was greater in the contralateral limb (β = 198.4 N, 95% CrI 171.6 to 225.1 N), in males (β = 184.3 N, 95% CrI 32.0 to 325.1 N), and with greater body mass (β = 119.9 N per 1-SD, 95% CrI 33.4 to 207.2 N). Greater relative MUAP amplitude was associated with lower firing rate (-3.7 Hz per 1-SD, 95% CrI -3.8 to -3.6 Hz).
CONCLUSIONS: Sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with later knee extensor strength, although a stronger positive association was suggested in the reconstructed limb at two weeks. Firing rate was strongly related to relative MUAP amplitude, and its predictive value for later strength appears limited.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

title: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy State of pathology: Insertional tendon tendinopathies.
abstract: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common but disabling pathology affecting both athletes and older subjects. The aim of the present study was to provide a practical review of IA, addressing the following questions: What are the etiologies and pathophysiology? Etiology is multifactorial, involving anatomic aspects and especially posterosuperior calcaneal prominence, biomechanical aspects such as short triceps surae, pes cavus or hindfoot varus, extrinsic aspects of footwear and overtraining, and metabolic aspects. Pathophysiology, depending on the individual case, implicates true insertional tendinopathy and posterior bone-tendon impingement to varying degrees, often with pre-Achilles bursitis; the distinction is crucial to decision-making. Impingement or enthesopathy lead to progressive disorganization of the collagen matrix, pathologic neovascularization and mucoid degeneration of the tendon, often with intratendon calcifications and inflammatory retrocalcaneal bursitis. How to establish diagnosis? Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on pain location, which is median in case of insertional tendinopathy and more lateral in case of posterior impingement with bursitis. Examination finds pain on palpation of the Achilles insertion, sometimes with local thickening, posterior tumefaction and painful restriction of ankle dorsiflexion. Tensing the tendon typically reproduces the pain. Functional tests may show restriction due to pain, without tendon tear. Weight-bearing X-ray, ultrasound and especially MRI analyze the respective roles of bone, tendon and bursa injury; weight-bearing CT can be contributive in some morphologically complex situations. Ultrasound reveals tendon thickening, hypoechogenic degenerative areas, hypervascularization on Doppler and associated bursitis. MRI shows lesion extension: intratendon degeneration, deep fiber involvement and retrocalcaneal inflammation. What are the non-operative treatments? Initial treatment is conservative, based on adapting weight-bearing and footwear, with exercises adapted to the form of the insertion, extracorporeal shock waves and rehabilitation. What are the surgical options and their expected results? In case of failure of well-conducted non-operative treatment, surgical strategy depends on lesion type, degree of posterior impingement, degree of tendon degeneration and degree of triceps surae stiffness. Expected results comprise pain relief, functional improvement on VISA-A score, and progressive return to activities, with timing depending on the technique and the initial level of activity. How to choose the surgical treatment? Surgical options comprise bone decompression, debridement and tendon reinsertion, flexor hallucis longus transfer and gastrocnemius lengthening depending on lesion type on clinical examination and imaging.

title: Effects of Fatigue on Peak and Angle-Specific Hamstring-to-Quadriceps Ratios in Collegiate Women Lacrosse Athletes.
abstract: Background: Hamstring strains and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears commonly occur in court and field sport athletes, with prevalence being higher in females. The likelihood of such injuries has been related to the hamstring-to-quadriceps (H:Q) strength ratio. Such a ratio can be affected by fatigue, to which athletes are frequently exposed. The aim of the current study was to investigate effects of fatigue on peak torque and angle-specific functional H:Q ratios at different angular velocities, as well as the association between resting functional H:Q ratios and those obtained following fatigue. Methods: A total of 18 collegiate women lacrosse players executed maximal knee concentric and eccentric contractions at angular velocities of 60, 180, and 240°/s following a supervised fatigue protocol. The isokinetic testing was then replicated. Results: There was a significant difference in functional peak torque H:Q ratios (p = 0.021-0.041) and ratios at 60 (p = 0.013-0.044), but not 20 degrees of knee flexion before and after fatigue at all three angular velocities. No main effects of angular velocity or ratio type were observed on H:Q ratio difference. The relationship between resting and fatigued functional H:Q ratios ranged from moderate to strong across all three angular velocities. Conclusions: Fatigue was associated with reductions in functional H:Q ratios, indicating altered knee flexor-extensor strength balance under fatigued conditions. In time-constrained settings, baseline functional H:Q ratio may provide practitioners with useful preliminary information regarding an athlete's potential susceptibility to lower-limb injury after fatigue.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

title: Tracking Recovery After TKA with Instrumented Timed Up and Go: Spatiotemporal, Rotational, and Strength Adaptations over Six Months.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability, and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) improves pain and functional mobility, although gait impairments may persist postoperatively. This study investigated longitudinal changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and gait performance using an instrumented Timed Up and Go (iTUG) test with wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). Twenty-two patients with end-stage KOA were assessed preoperatively and at 3, 12, and 24 weeks postoperatively. The Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score five-subscale composite (KOOS5) showed a significant overall change over time (p < 0.001), while isometric muscle strength showed significant overall changes across all tested muscle groups (p ≤ 0.008), with mean values demonstrating an initial postoperative decline followed by subsequent increases. Total TUG duration showed a significant overall time effect (p = 0.023), with significant reductions observed in the forward and return gait phases (p = 0.012 and p = 0.001, respectively). End-turning maximum rotational speed and sit-to-stand vertical acceleration showed significant overall time effects (p = 0.012 and p = 0.024, respectively), whereas the remaining parameters did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that recovery following TKA is multidimensional, with significant changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and functional mobility. iTUG analysis identified phase-specific changes, while several turning and transitional parameters did not show significant longitudinal changes, supporting the use of targeted rehabilitation strategies focusing on dynamic stability and movement control.

title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery.
DESCRIPTION: The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8.
RATIONALE: This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence.
IMPORTANT TIPS: The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: RICE = rest, ice, compression, elevationMRI = magnetic resonance imagingBID = twice daily.

title: Multi-Modal Biometric Fusion for Athletic Performance Optimization: Clinical Validation of the Dynamic Multi-Sensor Fusion Classifier (DMSFC).
abstract: Integrating real-time biometric monitoring into sports science is increasingly important for optimizing athletic performance and reducing injury risk. However, many existing systems have limited capacity to accurately combine data from multiple biometric sources. This study evaluated the Dynamic Multisensor Fusion (DMSFC) classifier for analyzing physiological and functional data collected from multiple biometric modalities, including electrocardiography (ECG), fingerprint measurements, and facial recognition. A multimodal biometric framework based on DMSFC was developed to monitor and classify key health and performance indicators in elite athletes. The variables evaluated included heart rate (HR), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure (BP), flexibility, muscle strength, and endurance capacity. The performance of the classifier was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). After implementing the proposed monitoring framework, improvements were observed in the evaluated performance and health indicators. The mean heart rate decreased from 78 to 66 beats per minute, while oxygen saturation slightly increased from 98% to 99%. Blood pressure decreased from 120/80 mmHg to 110/70 mmHg. Flexibility improved from 32 to 36 cm, muscle strength increased from 105 to 122 pounds, and endurance capacity increased from 20 to 24 minutes. Among the evaluated classifiers, DMSFC showed a strongest overall performance (i.e., accuracy of 0.94, sensitivity of 0.91, specificity of 0.96, and AUC of 0.97). These findings suggest that DMSFC could be capable of providing an effective framework for multimodal biometric analysis in sports science. Its use may support athlete assessment, facilitate the development of individualized training programs, and contribute to injury prevention strategies. Because the reported physiological changes were observed after implementation of the framework, further controlled studies are needed to determine whether they were caused by the monitoring system, the associated exercise program, or other factors.

title: Bony Anatomy, Soft-Tissue Adaptations and Neuromuscular Risk Factors of Shoulder Injury in Handball Players: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Handball is a high-intensity contact sport that imposes significant mechanical stress on the shoulder joint through repetitive, high-velocity overhead throwing, predisposing athletes to a wide spectrum of shoulder injuries. This narrative review examines the factors associated with shoulder injuries in handball players, highlighting underlying structural, adaptive and functional mechanisms across male and female athletes. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE was conducted to synthesize current evidence on bony anatomy, soft tissue adaptations and neuromuscular characteristics in handball cohorts. Factors associated with shoulder injury or symptoms can be broadly categorized into three conceptual domains: (i) bony anatomy and structural features, (ii) soft tissue adaptations and (iii) dynamic functional and neuromuscular factors. Bony factors include reduced acromiohumeral distance, increased humeral retrotorsion as a sport-specific skeletal adaptation and variations in glenoid morphology that may influence glenohumeral stability. Soft tissue adaptations include posterior capsular tightness, anterior capsular laxity and alterations in shoulder range of motion, particularly glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) accompanied by external rotation gain (ERG), which may influence glenohumeral kinematics and potentially contribute to shoulder symptoms or overuse conditions. Beyond these structural features, dynamic functional factors, including shoulder rotator muscle strength imbalances, impaired scapular control and training-load management, play a central role in injury development. Therefore, a comprehensive assessment encompassing anatomical correlates, soft tissue characteristics and functional/neuromuscular characteristics may support the development of targeted injury-prevention and rehabilitation strategies in handball players.

title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
abstract: Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: Arthroscopic Circumferential Labral Repair and Biceps Tenodesis in Elite Throwing Athletes: Technical Considerations.
abstract: SLAP lesions are a common cause of shoulder pain in overhead athletes and are often seen together with circumferential labral tearing, partial-thickness rotator cuff tearing, and biceps pathology. Isolated repair of the superior labrum has produced inconsistent outcomes, with low return-to-play rates in professional throwers. In patients with these complex cases, instability and anterior shoulder pain often coexist, and isolated labral repair or tenodesis may not be adequate treatment. Conversely, tenodesis without superior labral repair may increase glenohumeral translation. The senior author believes long head of the biceps tendon release reduces traction on the SLAP repair and may support healing. We describe an arthroscopic technique for circumferential labral repair, with knotless all-suture anchors performed in the beach-chair position, combined with open subpectoral biceps tenodesis and adjunct subacromial decompression. This technique restores stability, removes the biceps as a pain generator, eliminates traction on the repaired labrum, and preserves motion.

title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects.
METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented.
RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program.
CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

title: Toward Wearable Joint Load Monitoring: Concurrent Estimation of Hip, Knee, and Ankle Sagittal Contact Forces from Sparse IMU Measurements.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Continuous monitoring of lower extremity joint contact forces is critical for rehabilitation medicine, sports injury prevention, and assistive device development. Yet, current wearable solutions often lack multi-joint integration or require cumbersome sensor arrays. This study aims to concurrently estimate hip, knee, and ankle sagittal compressive contact forces using a sparse inertial measurement unit (IMU) configuration across diverse daily activities.
METHODS: We collected data from 14 healthy adults equipped with four IMU sensors performing various daily movements, with reference contact forces captured using optical motion capture and force platforms. To estimate joint contact forces, we developed a domain-informed multi-task temporal convolutional network (Ada-Att-MTCN). This architecture integrates a shared temporal convolutional network encoder, task-specific attention mechanisms, homoscedastic uncertainty-based dynamic task weighting, and a soft physiological-bound penalty. Performance was evaluated using 14-fold leave-one-subject-out nested cross-validation against 4 baseline methods, with root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) as evaluation metrics.
RESULTS: On the self-collected dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN achieved the highest accuracy across all activities, with mean RMSEs of 0.328 ± 0.13 BW (hip), 0.380 ± 0.09 BW (knee), and 0.365 ± 0.15 BW (ankle), and an average R2 of 0.822 ± 0.10. On the external dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN likewise performed best among all methods (average R² = 0.754 ± 0.05).
CONCLUSION: The proposed framework captures complex inter-joint dynamics, enabling robust simultaneous load estimation with drastically reduced hardware complexity.
SIGNIFICANCE: This approach provides a practical, non-invasive solution for transitioning lab-grade multi-joint load monitoring to wearable deployment in rehabilitation and sports medicine.

title: Should athletes take omega-3 supplements? Current evidence for recovery, adaptation and performance.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To evaluate whether long-chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation provides meaningful benefits for recovery, training adaptation or performance in athletic populations, while distinguishing mechanistic plausibility from demonstrated functional effects.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent data from athletic populations show that Omega-3 Index (O3I) values commonly fall below proposed cardioprotective thresholds, although athlete-specific targets remain unvalidated. Meta-analyses and controlled trials suggest that supplementation may modestly reduce muscle soreness and attenuate selected losses of muscle function following damaging exercise. However, findings are inconsistent across formulations, doses and outcomes, and benefits do not translate reliably into improved strength, endurance, power or sport performance. Evidence concerning female, masters and contact-sport athletes is limited.
SUMMARY: Routine supplementation cannot at present be recommended for all athletes. Targeted supplementation may be considered following dietary and, wherever appropriate, biomarker assessment, while recognizing that benefits during unusually damaging or congested training remain unproven.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.
