title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Effect of Pulsed Electromagnetic Stimulation on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The effect of pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy on muscle performance and serum creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Mb) values - the biomarkers of muscle damage in experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) - has yet to be investigated. PEMF therapy is known to be effective to reduce muscle pain, muscle recovery time, fatigue but not to increase muscle force production. The study aimed to compare the effect of PEMF and sham therapy on experimentally induced DOMS in sedentary undergraduate college students.
HYPOTHESIS: PEMF therapy would improve pain, pressure pain threshold (PPT), functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration compared with the sham intervention.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, participant- and assessor-blinded, sham-controlled study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: This study was conducted at Pamukkale University Sarayköy Vocational School. A total of 52 healthy sedentary people received 3 consecutive days of active (Experimental group, n = 26) or sham (Sham group, n = 26) PEMF therapy 24 hours after DOMS induction with a drop-jump protocol. Pain intensity, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration were assessed at baseline, 24 hours and 72 hours after DOMS induction protocol.
RESULTS: The drop-jump protocol induced DOMS successfully in both groups (P < 0.05). All outcome measures were improved in the experimental group (P < 0.05). Mean change scores of PPT (P = 0.53), functional performance (P = 0.10), serum CK (P = 0.38), and Mb concentrations (P = 0.08) were not significantly different between baseline and 72 hours in the sham group. Statistically significant decreases in Mb concentrations were determined in the sham group (P = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration. The duration of PEMF therapy was sufficient to resolve the PPT, functional performance, and serum CK and Mb concentrations associated with DOMS.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study adds to existing knowledge in showing that, compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration.

title: A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical Outcomes.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries were historically managed nonsurgically or with primary repairs, owing to limited anatomic knowledge, subjective diagnostic techniques, and nonvalidated reconstructions that frequently failed. We describe a two-decade, bench-to-bedside PCL research pyramid that progressively addressed these deficiencies. Foundational cadaveric work characterized the quantitative anatomy of the PCL, including the anterolateral and posteromedial bundles, yielding reproducible femoral and tibial osseous landmarks for tunnel placement. Robotic biomechanical testing established the codominant contribution of both bundles, optimal graft fixation angles, and the destabilizing influence of posterolateral corner injuries and flat tibial slope. Objective diagnostic methods, such as kneeling PCL stress radiography and posterior tibial translation on MRI, were validated to quantify laxity and detect chronic tears. These insights informed an anatomically grounded double-bundle reconstruction, complemented by multiligament tunnel convergence-avoidance strategies, evidence-based tensioning sequences, and a refined rehabilitation and bracing treatment protocol. Prospective outcome studies confirmed restoration of stability comparable to anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions, demonstrating how integrated translational research transformed treatment of this challenging injury.

title: Editorial Commentary: Basketball Players Return to Sport at a High Rate-Now We Must Embrace the Challenge of Reporting Longer-Term Outcomes and Identifying Predisposing Factors for Hip Pathology!
abstract: Athletes of all kinds, including basketball players, undergoing hip arthroscopy have been shown to have generally good outcomes and return to sport at a high rate. title: Transient ST-T Changes During Submaximal Exercise Revealing Anomalous Right Coronary Artery Origin in an Asymptomatic Athlete.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery is a recognised structural cause of sudden cardiac death in athletes younger than 35 years. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic prior to cardiac events, and resting and exercise electrocardiography (ECG) findings are frequently normal or non-specific, limiting the effectiveness of preparticipation screening.
CASE SUMMARY: We report a case of a 22-year-old asymptomatic athlete in whom preparticipation screening revealed transient ST-segment depression and T-wave inversions during submaximal exercise and recovery, whereas findings at peak exercise remained normal. Point-of-care echocardiography performed by a sports medicine specialist raised suspicion of an anomalous origin of the right coronary artery from the left aortic sinus of Valsalva, which was subsequently confirmed by computed tomography coronary angiography. High-risk anatomical features included an acute ostial angle and an interarterial course of the right coronary artery. Functional testing with exercise myocardial stress scintigraphy showed no inducible perfusion defect. Following multidisciplinary consultation, a conservative management strategy with activity modification and close follow-up was adopted.
DISCUSSION: This case highlights the potential clinical significance of transient ST-T abnormalities occurring during submaximal exercise and recovery, even in the absence of symptoms or abnormalities at peak workload. In this patient, recognition of this reproducible but non-specific ECG pattern prompted further structural evaluation leading to the diagnosis of AAOCA. It also underscores the limitations of current guidelines in managing asymptomatic athletes with high-risk coronary anatomy but without evidence of inducible ischaemia, supporting the need for individualised decision-making.

title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: Bilateral Lower-Body Force Asymmetry and Countermovement Jump Performance of South African Amateur Padel Athletes.
abstract: The countermovement jump (CMJ) is a widely used assessment of lower-limb power and neuromuscular function. The physical demands of padel, including repeated accelerations, decelerations, changes of direction, jumping, and landing, may contribute to inter-limb asymmetries influencing performance and injury risk. This quantitative cross-sectional study investigated lower-limb asymmetries during the CMJ in amateur (non-professional) padel athletes. Thirty participants (mean age: 41.2 ± 14.5 years; 63% male, 37% female) completed bilateral CMJ assessments using VALD (Brisbane, Australia) ForceDecks force plates. Outcome measures included concentric, eccentric, and landing peak force, peak power, rate of force development and jump height. Significant dominant-limb advantages were identified for concentric (p = 0.002), eccentric (p = 0.024), and landing peak force (p = 0.044). Male athletes demonstrated greater jump heights than female athletes (p < 0.001), while female athletes exhibited greater landing-phase force asymmetry (p = 0.004). Amateur padel athletes display significant inter-limb asymmetries in force production across the concentric, eccentric, and landing phases of the CMJ, with greater force generation in the dominant limb. Furthermore, the greater landing asymmetry observed in female athletes may reflect reduced inter-limb load distribution during landing tasks. These results highlight the value of CMJ assessment in identifying neuromuscular asymmetries that may influence performance and increase injury risk in padel athletes.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: Exercise Is Associated with Skeletal Muscle Autophagy-Lysosome-Related Markers and Nrf2/ARF1 Signaling in HFD Mice.
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate the protective effects and potential mechanisms of exercise against long-term high-fat diet (HFD)-induced skeletal muscle dysfunction, with a focus on ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1)-related autophagy-lysosome markers and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) signaling. Methods: Forty male C57BL/6 mice were randomly divided into a normal diet group (DC) and an HFD group, and the latter was further subdivided into a model group (MG), exercise group (EG), Nrf2 inhibitor group (NG), and exercise combined with Nrf2 inhibitor group (ENG) after 12 weeks of HFD feeding. EG received 6 weeks of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise, NG was treated with Nrf2 inhibitor for 6 weeks, and ENG received both the 6-week treadmill exercise and inhibitor injections simultaneously. Serum lipid, blood glucose and insulin resistance indices were detected; skeletal muscle morphology was observed by H&E staining; mRNA and protein expression of ARF1, ULK1, ATP6V0A1 and other factors were determined by RT-qPCR, Western blotting and immunohistochemistry; the oxidative stress index was measured by an ELISA; and the colocalization of ARF1/ATP6V0A1 with the lysosomal marker Lamp1 was analyzed by immunofluorescence. Results: Long-term HFD significantly increased mouse body weight, serum TC, TG, LDL-C, FBG levels and the HOMA-IR index, induced morphological alterations in skeletal muscle (loose myofiber arrangement, abundant intracellular vacuoles), inhibited the mRNA expression of ARF1, ULK1 and ATP6V0A1, and elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) content (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Six weeks of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise effectively improved HFD-induced metabolic disorders and skeletal muscle morphological damage, upregulated the expression of ARF1, ULK1 and ATP6V0A1, and reduced oxidative stress (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Notably, luteolin-mediated inhibition of Nrf2 signaling may partially reverse exercise-induced alterations in ARF1-related autophagy-lysosome markers and skeletal muscle morphology. Conclusions: Long-term HFD may induce morphological alterations in skeletal muscle, accompanied by changes in ARF1-associated autophagy-lysosome markers and elevated oxidative stress. Conversely, moderate-intensity exercise may ameliorate HFD-related changes in skeletal muscle morphology, potentially via Nrf2 signaling, providing a potential molecular target and theoretical basis for the exercise intervention strategies against HFD-induced metabolic-related skeletal muscle dysfunction.

title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults.
METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions.
RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h.
CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

title: Post-COVID-19 Penalty Trends Following an Injury-Prevention Rule Change in Rhode Island High School Boys' Hockey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Penalty infraction minute (PIM)-based rule modifications have been implemented in youth and high school ice hockey to reduce injury risk. A prior Rhode Island Interscholastic League (RIIL) study demonstrated a reduction in game-related injuries following implementation of a statewide 2015-2016 50/70 PIM rule. The durability of these behavioral trends post-COVID-19 has not been evaluated.
PURPOSE: This descriptive epidemiologic study evaluates post-pandemic trends in penalty infraction minutes and disqualifying penalties in RIIL boys' varsity ice hockey.
METHODS: Publicly available RIIL varsity boys' ice hockey data were reviewed for four consecutive seasons (2021-2022 through 2024-2025). Extracted variables included total rostered players, counts of players exceeding PIM thresholds (≥25, ≥50, ≥70), mean team PIM per game, goals scored, number of participating teams, and total disqualifying penalties per season. Data were summarized descriptively by season.
RESULTS: Across four seasons, rostered players ranged from 479 to 540, with 21 to 25 teams competing annually. Mean team PIM per game remained stable, ranging from 8.13 to 8.83. No players accumulated ≥50 or ≥70 PIM in any season. Players accumulating ≥25 PIM ranged from 17 to 24 per season. Disqualifying penalties occurred each season (range, 5-11 per year) without a consistent directional trend. Goals scored remained proportional to participating teams.
CONCLUSIONS: In post-pandemic seasons, PIM distributions and disqualifying penalties remained stable, with no recurrence of high-PIM accumulations requiring suspension. These findings suggest sustained behavioral patterns following rule modifications, but cannot be interpreted as evidence of injury reduction without injury surveillance data. Continued monitoring incorporating injury outcomes is warranted.

title: Breaking limits: rapid sea-to-summit ascent of Mount Everest (8,848 m) in 3 days 23 hours following normobaric-hypoxic pre-acclimatization and staged supplemental oxygen in a non-elite athlete.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Traditional ascent of Mount Everest (8,848 m) typically requires 40-50 days of on-mountain acclimatization. Normobaric hypoxia (NH) pre-acclimatization is a practical home-based alternative; however, no peer-reviewed case report has described a sea-to-summit Everest ascent completed in under four days by a non-elite individual without prior on-mountain acclimatization rotations.
METHODS: A 40-year-old male recreational mountaineer (baseline VO2max 40.8 ml·kg-1·min-1; BMI 30.1 kg·m-2) completed an 18-week structured NH pre-acclimatization program comprising 48 nights of hypoxic sleep (~377 h at simulated altitudes of 1,850-5,486 m; FiO2 16.7-10.5%) and 16 hypoxic exercise sessions (34 h at 3,085-6,000 m; FiO2 14.3-9.8%). Hypoxic dose was calculated as Σ[(95/SpO2 - 1) × h × 100]. During the climb, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate (HR) were recorded at each camp, and acute mountain sickness (AMS) was assessed using the 2018 Lake Louise Score (LLS). Supplemental oxygen (O2) was initiated at 0.5 L·min-1 at the start of the ascent from Everest Base Camp (EBC, 5,360 m) and titrated to SpO2 and symptoms up to 3.0 L·min-1 during the summit push.
RESULTS: The program yielded a combined hypoxic exposure of 411 h and a cumulative hypoxic dose of 4,779%·h (sleep 4,353%·h; exercise 426%·h). VO2max increased from 40.8 to 51.0 ml·kg-1·min-1, and body mass decreased from 118.1 to 101.5 kg. The subject departed New York at 00:30 local time (EDT; 10:15 Nepal Standard Time, NST) on 15 May 2025 and reached the summit at 09:22 NST on 19 May 2025, a total sea-to-summit time of 3 days, 23 hours and 7 minutes; the ascent from EBC to the summit took 60 hours and 22 minutes. SpO2 was 75% at Camp 3 (7,100 m; HR 95 bpm) and 70% on arrival at Camp 4 (7,950 m; HR 105 bpm) and at the summit (HR 105 bpm). On descent, SpO2 recovered to 80% at Camp 4 and 85% at Camp 2 (6,750 m; HR 110 bpm), and was 85% on room air on return to EBC (HR 62 bpm). No AMS was diagnosed during the ascent (LLS 0-1 at all ascending checkpoints); mild AMS criteria were met on descent (LLS = 3), resolving by return to EBC. No high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary edema occurred.
DISCUSSION: To our knowledge, this case documents the fastest recorded sea-to-summit ascent of Mount Everest by a non-professional athlete. The combination of a structured 18-week NH pre-acclimatization program, objective physiological monitoring, and staged supplemental oxygen, together with the absence of severe altitude-related complications, suggests that rapid ascent without traditional on-mountain acclimatization may be feasible in a well-prepared, closely supervised non-elite individual. Controlled prospective studies are required to quantify the relative contributions of hematological, ventilatory, and mitochondrial adaptations induced by high-dose NH exposure.

title: Progression of peak athletic performance age in the past four decades.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Older athletes are redefining the prime by extending their athletic longevity. A trend that women's peak performance age tends to increase, while men's remains largely unchanged, has been reported some time ago. The present study builds on this early work by examining more recent data to determine whether such gender differences persisted across contemporary periods and in different sporting events.
METHODS: Ages of Olympic medalists from 1984 to 2024 were analyzed as indicators of peak performance age (N.=2016).
RESULTS: In men, peak performance ages ranged 26±2 to 28±2 years in endurance, 26±2 to 27±2 years in power, 23±1 to 24±2 years in sprint, and 26±2 to 27±2 years in skill. In women, the ranges were from 27±2 to 29±2 years for endurance, 26±2 to 28±2 years for power, 23±2 to 24±2 years for sprint, and 23±3 to 26±3 years for skill. There were no gender differences in peak performance age among endurance, power, and sprint events in any era. However, in skill sports, male athletes demonstrated a higher peak performance age in 1984-1996 (P<0.05), a difference that has since disappeared. The age variabilities show an upward trend over time in both men and women.
CONCLUSIONS: We concluded that in recent years, both male and female athletes have achieved peak performance at comparable ages across all sport types.

title: Creative Solution for Recurrent Failure of Flexor Tendon Repair.
abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

title: Investigational Peptides in Orthopaedic Practice: Evidence, Safety, and Patient Counseling for BPC-157, Thymosin Beta-4, and TB-500.
abstract: Peptide-based products, particularly Body Protection Compound-157 (BPC-157), and thymosin beta-4 (TB-4), and products marketed as TB-500, are increasingly promoted for musculoskeletal recovery despite limited clinical validation. This narrative review evaluated their molecular rationale, direct musculoskeletal evidence, human safety and efficacy data, product quality concerns, regulatory status, antidoping implications, and relevance to orthopaedic counseling. PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Scopus were searched from inception through June 2026, with additional review of primary regulatory and antidoping sources. BPC-157 has the largest bod of direct musculoskeletal preclinical evidence, including predominantly small-animal studies involving tendon, ligament, muscle, inflammatory joint disease, and bone. However, human musculoskeletal evidence is limited to one small retrospective uncontrolled case series without validated outcome measures. Validated dosing, pharmacokinetic, and long-term safety data are lacking. TB-4 has broader experimental and human experience in ophthalmic, dermatologic, and cardiovascular applications, but direct musculoskeletal evidence remains limited to in vitro and rodent studies. These nonorthopaedic findings cannot establish musculoskeletal efficacy or safety. TB-500 is a distinct seven amino-acid fragment of TB-4 that is frequently conflated with full-length TB-4 despite the absence of validated biologic or clinical equivalence. Commercial products marketed also raise concerns regarding identity, purity, concentration, sterility, and manufacturing consistency. None of these agents has an FDA-approved musculoskeletal indication, validated orthopaedic treatment protocol, or controlled human orthopaedic efficacy evidence. Orthopaedic clinicians should specifically ask about peptide use, distinguish preclinical plausibility from clinical validation, address product quality and safety uncertainties, and counsel athletes regarding antidoping restrictions. Routine clinical use cannot be currently recommended.

title: Editorial Commentary: High Failure Rate of All-Inside Hamstring Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction at Long-Term Follow-Up: It's the Graft Not the Construct, but the Future Keeps Complicating the Past.
abstract: Recent reports of high failure rates after all-inside hamstring autograft anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction have renewed an old debate: is the problem the graft, the construct, or both? Interpretation is difficult because hamstring anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction has evolved alongside changes in graft configuration, socket drilling, and adjustable-loop cortical fixation. Potential contributors include graft elongation, unequal strand loading, adjustable-loop lengthening, and the longer working length of cortical fixation. Yet higher revision rates with hamstring autografts were identified before widespread adoption of the modern all-inside technique, suggesting that fixation alone does not explain the signal. Meanwhile, all-inside techniques have increasingly been paired with quadriceps tendon autograft without the same apparent failure concern. The literature remains messy, but the simplest explanation may still be the correct one: hamstring autograft itself appears less forgiving in higher-risk patients. For those patients, quadriceps or patellar tendon autograft remains the more reliable choice.

title: Cartilage-targeting engineered probiotic bacterial extracellular vesicles treat osteoarthritis through modulation of matrix homeostasis.
abstract: Reversing extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolic dysregulation to facilitate cartilage repair represents a key therapeutic strategy for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment. Owing to the avascular nature of joint structures, intra-articular injection is a commonly used clinical administration route. However, the current drug retention time is insufficient to effectively reverse OA progression. In this study, we demonstrated that natural bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are capable of repairing cartilage damage. We modified Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)-derived BEVs with a chondrocyte-targeting peptide to prolong their therapeutic efficacy. Engineered BEVs, as a drug delivery system, are capable of continuously transporting endogenous miRNAs. Cartilage-targeting LGG-EVs (W-LGG-EVs) penetrate deeply into cartilage tissue and promote extracellular matrix secretion by chondrocytes. Furthermore, W-LGG-EVs were shown to restore cartilage homeostasis and ultimately alleviate stress-related OA. BEVs, as a novel and safe therapeutic agent, hold clinical feasibility.

title: The Influence of Sleep and Autonomic Recovery on Performance in World-Class Swimmers at Major Competitions: The Qualifying Trials, World Championships, and Olympic Games.
abstract: Sleep deprivation is one of the main risk factors for impaired performance in elite athletes, but the changes in sleep and autonomic regulation in response to competitions of varying levels within the same Olympic year remain unknown. In this prospective, longitudinal, observational study, we monitored parameters related to sleep quality and quantity, as well as heart rate variability and resting heart rate, in a cohort of eight Olympic swimmers (n = 8) during the World Championships in Doha, the qualifying trials, and the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, using the Oura Ring Gen3 under real-world conditions throughout the pre-competition, competition, and post-competition phases of each event. The Olympic Games were the only event where sleep efficiency fell below the commonly used reference threshold of 85% during the competition phase accompanied by a reduction in the total sleep score and an increase in resting heart rate. The Olympic setting was accompanied by temporary changes in sleep and autonomic markers, but no sleep parameter or autonomic marker showed a statistically significant association with intra-individual competitive performance, although the limited sample size constrains the power to detect such relationships.

title: Long-Term Fitness Profile and Performance-Related Indicators in Semi-Professional Female Handball Players.
abstract: Long-term, single-club datasets linking fitness and match performance are rare in women's handball. This retrospective study profiled fitness and game-quality indicators across 14 seasons (2010-2022, 2026; N = 45; 8-17 players/season). Anthropometric and specific-fitness values (height 173.90 ± 5.53 cm, body mass 68.28 ± 8.08 kg, jump-throw velocity 79.94 ± 6.83 km/h, countermovement jump 43.46 ± 4.84 cm, VO2max 48.01 ± 3.61 mL/kg/min) were sub-elite. Shot efficiency (55.74 ± 6.00%) approached elite values (58.90 ± 7.60%). Backs were older, more experienced, and higher-scoring than Wings and Pivots. Universal players matched Backs' output despite being younger and less experienced. Experience correlated with goals per match (r = 0.51, p = 0.001), positive actions (r = 0.44, p = 0.005), and action balance (r = 0.47, p = 0.003). Throwing velocity and sprint/agility speed showed similar associations. Endurance, strength, and coordination/dribble deficit showed none. Fitness indicators improved across 2010-2022, but a single season after near-complete roster turnover departed markedly from this trend. Trends should not be extrapolated to a changed roster without retesting. A small set of trainable, sport-specific qualities, not general fitness, best predicts match performance. Findings provide normative benchmarks and training priorities for coaches.

title: The enhanced rehabilitation programme for significant musculoskeletal injuries from the manchester arena bombing - A process evaluation study investigating patients' and physiotherapists' experiences.
abstract: The 2017 Manchester Arena bombing exposed major gaps in the UK's civilian trauma rehabilitation services. In response, the Enhanced Rehabilitation after Major Trauma Programme (ERP), a structured, multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach, was developed by the NHS, in collaboration with the Universities of Manchester and Salford, and the Manchester Institute of Health and Performance (MIHP). This study employed the Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) framework to evaluate the integration and impact of ERP from the perspectives of physiotherapists and patients. Thirteen patients and four physiotherapists participated in semi-structured interviews and a focus group. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) and then deductively with NPT constructs. Both groups regarded ERP as a valuable alternative to standard NHS rehabilitation. Its structured, multidisciplinary design supported physical and psychological recovery, improved motivation, and enhanced physiotherapist expertise. However, concerns were raised about sustaining progress after ERP, difficulties transitioning back to NHS care, and the absence of long-term rehabilitation pathways. Despite its positive outcomes, the wider adoption of ERP in the NHS faces barriers, including limited resources and systemic constraints. This study demonstrates the potential of structured rehabilitation models for trauma survivors. Future research should explore cost-effective ways to sustain and expand enhanced trauma rehabilitation.

title: Pre-season friendly match-play as a double-edged sword: Performance gains and inflammatory cost in semi-professional soccer players (a natural experiment).
abstract: Pre-season training prepares soccer players for competition, but the longitudinal effects of friendly match exposure remain unclear. We investigated whether cumulative late pre-season match-play is associated with physiological adaptation in semi-professional players. Twenty-four male players from a randomly selected semi-professional team competing at national level were assessed at pre-season start, mid-pre-season and pre-competition. Measurements included body composition, physical performance, aerobic fitness and blood markers reflecting muscle damage, inflammation, hormonal status and haematological adaptation. Based on cumulative playing time across eight friendly matches, as determined by coaching staff, players were classified retrospectively into extended play (EP) or limited play (LP) groups. Controlling for mid-pre-season baseline, the EP group showed significantly lower pre-competition values for body mass ( η p 2 = 0.276), body fat ( η p 2 = 0.294) and 35 m sprint time ( η p 2 = 0.129) and higher values for lower-limb power (dominant/non-dominant; η p 2 = 0.219-0.424), velocity at maximal oxygen uptake ( η p 2 = 0.441) and at second ventilatory threshold ( η p 2 = 0.708), serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase ( η p 2 = 0.296), myoglobin ( η p 2 = 0.199), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein ( η p 2 = 0.920), interleukin-6 ( η p 2 = 0.893), tumour necrosis factor-α ( η p 2 = 0.937) and red blood cell count ( η p 2 = 0.190) (all P ≤ 0.038). Across all participants, total match-play time was correlated significantly with reductions in body fat (r = -0.47) and increases in lower-limb power (r = 0.44-0.67), second ventilatory threshold (r = 0.55) and inflammatory markers (r = 0.79-0.86) (all P ≤ 0.033). Greater friendly match-play exposure during pre-season was associated with favourable physiological adaptations and a more pronounced physiological and inflammatory response. These findings support friendly match-play as a meaningful physiological stimulus and highlight the importance of balancing match exposure with recovery during pre-season preparation.

title: Intensity-dependent microcurrent stimulation enhances BMSC-derived cartilage microtissue formation under defined culture conditions.
abstract: Engineering phenotypically favorable cartilage-like tissue from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) remains challenging because chondrogenic differentiation can be accompanied by insufficient cartilage-associated extracellular matrix accumulation and unfavorable hypertrophic and catabolic responses. Here, we established a microcurrent-assisted culture system for scaffold-free BMSC-derived cartilage microtissues (CMTs) and investigated the intensity-dependent effects of continuous unidirectional direct-current stimulation at 0, 50, 100, 150, 250, or 500 μA under a defined electrical and culture configuration. Among the tested conditions, 150 μA (nominal electrode current density, 3 μA/mm2) showed the most consistently favorable overall response, with enhanced cartilage-associated gene and protein expression, greater type II collagen- and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix accumulation, improved CMT morphology, and higher apparent mechanical properties. In contrast, 250 and 500 μA were associated with reduced cartilage-associated matrix formation and increased fibrotic, hypertrophic, catabolic, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related markers. The 150 μA condition was also associated with a distinct intracellular Ca2+ response pattern and increased NFATc1 nuclear localization; verapamil, BAPTA-AM, and cyclosporin A attenuated NFATc1 nuclear localization, supporting involvement of Ca2+/calcineurin/NFAT-related signaling without establishing a unique causal mechanism. After 2 weeks of xenogeneic subcutaneous implantation in nude mice, CMTs preconditioned at 150 μA exhibited greater cartilage-like matrix accumulation and higher apparent compressive properties than those preconditioned at 0 or 500 μA. These findings identify 150 μA as the best-performing tested condition under the present electrical configuration and provide short-term ectopic proof-of-concept evidence, while longer-term orthotopic studies are required to evaluate phenotypic stability, tissue integration, and functional outcomes in cartilage-defect models.

title: A rare traumatic triad: Open bicondylar non-conjoint Hoffa fracture with partial tibial tubercle and medial epicondyle avulsions - A case report and biomechanical analysis.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles are rare intra-articular injuries, and the simultaneous occurrence of a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture with a partial anterior tibial tubercle avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion constitutes an exceptionally complex traumatic triad. We report the case of a 35-year-old male motorcyclist who sustained this "floating" articular block injury (AO/OTA 33-B3.3) following a high-velocity accident. Diagnostic assessment utilizing Computed Tomography with 3D reconstruction revealed a vertical Letenneur Type II fracture of the medial condyle and a comminuted Letenneur Type I fracture of the lateral condyle, complicated by significant rotational instability. Surgical management prioritized the posterior femoral instability through a double posterior approach, which allowed for direct visualization and anatomical reduction. Fixation was achieved using posterior-to-anterior headless compression screws, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to neutralize shear forces, while the medial epicondyle was anatomically reduced and fixed; the stable partial tibial tubercle avulsion was treated conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient demonstrated excellent functional recovery with 120 degrees of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a successful return to recreational sports. This case highlights the importance of the double posterior approach and "targeted rigidity" in managing multidirectional instability, permitting early mobilization even in the presence of complex extensor mechanism involvement.
INTRODUCTION: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles (Hoffa fractures) are rare intra-articular injuries, with bicondylar patterns being exceptionally uncommon. A non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture combined with a partial anterior tibial tubercle (ATT) avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion represents a complex, "floating" articular block that challenges standard treatment algorithms. This case report analyzes the biomechanics and management of this rare traumatic triad.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 35-year-old male motorcyclist presented with a Gustilo-Anderson Type I open knee injury following a high-velocity crash involving hyper-flexion and valgus stress. CT imaging confirmed a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture (AO/OTA 33-B3.3, Bagaria Type 3). The lateral condyle presented as a Letenneur Type I fracture with extensive comminution, while the medial condyle was a Letenneur Type II vertical fracture. Associated injuries included an Ogden Type I partial ATT avulsion and a Watson-Jones Type I medial epicondyle avulsion.Surgical management utilized a double posterior approach to visualize and reduce the posterior fragments. Fixation involved headless cannulated compression screws for both condyles, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to resist shear forces. The medial epicondyle was refixed with a screw and washer, while the stable ATT avulsion was managed conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient achieved excellent functional outcomes, including 120° of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a Tegner Activity Scale score of 7.
CONCLUSION: Managing this complex triad requires a thorough understanding of the injury mechanism, which involves coronal shear, valgus stress, and eccentric extensor loading. 3D CT reconstruction is mandatory for planning, and a double posterior approach provides superior visualization for anatomical reduction and posterior-to-anterior fixation. Rigid fixation, particularly using anti-glide plating for the lateral column, permits early mobilization and the conservative management of stable associated injuries, leading to high patient satisfaction.

title: Extracting meaningful features from time series analysis of plasma analytes in clinical research.
abstract: While absolute blood biomarkers have long guided diagnosis, their rate of change often provides greater diagnostic value. For the Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophies studied here, increased muscle weakness is associated with abnormal sarcolemma repair. Time course analyses were made to changes in muscle-derived plasma enzymes after modest physical activity of ambulatory inpatients. Blood samples at 20 selected time points at variable intervals were obtained at rest, and before and after routine morning activities and motor function testing. After these activities, plasma enzyme levels increased in a similar way, suggesting damage and leakage from skeletal muscle. The levels then decreased in a similar way, suggesting that muscle cells stopped leaking and enzymes were subsequently cleared from the blood. The complex temporal changes were modeled using both continuous time and data features to reduce the number of parameters required to describe the irregularly sampled, interrupted, time series data. Unlike individuals with cardiac muscle ischemia or following intense exercise, there was no extended post-injury rising phase of enzyme levels. In contradistinction, levels fell once activity ceased. Time series analyses of blood biomarkers most likely provide an assay and index of sarcolemma fragility and by extension skeletal muscle damage.

title: Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery: Are Marathon and Trail Running Different?
abstract: Although trail and road are two running disciplines, they have distinct characteristics potentially leading to different physiological impacts that have never been examined. The aim of the present study was to compare neuromuscular fatigue and recovery between a marathon and two trail runs of equivalent effort (29 km; ± 1,400 m). Forty-one trained runners, specialized in either road or trail running, performed a simulated treadmill marathon (MARASIM), a simulated treadmill trail run (TRAILSIM), or a trail run in natural conditions (TRAILNAT), depending on their speciality. Neuromuscular fatigue, i.e. changes in maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), voluntary activation (VA) and peak twitch (Tw) of the knee extensors (KE) and plantar flexors (PF), blood markers of muscle damage, jump performance, and force-velocity profile (FVP) were assessed before (PRE), immediately after (POST), one (+1 day), two (+2 days), and seven days (+7 days) following the runs. Muscle pain questionnaires were administered at PRE and during the month following the run. MARASIM showed significantly greater decreases in KE VA (-23.5% vs. -9.2% vs. -13.0%) and jump height (-11.7%; +11.4%; +5.9%, for squat jump), and significantly higher increases in blood markers of muscle damage (+1,726 UI.L -1; +641 UI.L -1; +363 UI.L -1; at +1 day) compared to TRAILSIM and TRAILNAT, respectively. The return to baseline occurred later in MARASIM for KE VA and jump height. Muscle soreness values also returned to baseline earlier in TRAILNAT and TRAILSIM compared to MARASIM. No differences between groups existed in KE Pt and MVC, in any PF neuromuscular fatigue variables, and FVP. Overall, marathon running appears to induce greater acute neuromuscular alterations than trail running, mostly on KE, with a slower return to baseline values.

title: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells and regenerative medicine.
abstract: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) continue to drive innovation in regenerative medicine, yet the field is undergoing a critical evolution from the early concept of cellular engraftment to complex paracrine-mediated tissue repair. This review systematically evaluates the core scientific questions defining this transition, highlighting the latest advancements in MSC biology and the rapidly expanding therapeutic frontier of MSC-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs). We critically appraise recent progress in decoding MSC therapeutic mechanisms, specifically their profound capacity for immune modulation and microenvironmental remodeling. By synthesizing current findings across diverse and challenging clinical applications-encompassing oral tissue regeneration, osteoarthritis, and complex immune disorders-we provide expert insights into the discrepancies between promising preclinical data and variable clinical outcomes. Crucially, we address persistent translational bottlenecks, including inherent donor heterogeneity, manufacturing scalability, and the lack of standardized potency assays. It is our perspective that overcoming these limitations demands a strategic pivot towards precise cell-free MSC-EV therapies and advanced bioengineering strategies. Ultimately, this review highlights key directions for future research. By connecting basic mechanistic insights with clinical demands, we aim to accelerate the translation of effective MSC-based therapies.

title: Sleep, Chronotype and Physiological Acclimatisation During a 21-Day Altitude Training Camp in World-Class Swimmers.
abstract: Altitude training is widely used in elite swimming, although its effects on sleep and acclimatisation remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this study was to describe changes in sleep difficulty, physiological acclimatisation, athlete-reported outcomes, and haematological markers during a 21-day altitude training camp (2320 m), and to explore the association between chronotype and sleep difficulty. Seven world-class swimmers (4 men, 3 women) were monitored before, during, and after altitude exposure. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire, while daily monitoring included resting oxygen saturation, resting heart rate, acute mountain sickness symptoms, fatigue, recovery, hydration status, and training load. Chronotype was determined using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire. Sleep difficulty was descriptively higher during the first week at altitude (6.14 ± 1.07 vs. 4.14 ± 1.21 at baseline) and returned towards baseline by week 3 (4.29 ± 1.50), although pairwise comparisons did not remain significant after multiplicity correction. Strong inverse associations between chronotype and sleep difficulty were observed at baseline (rho = -0.87, p = 0.014) and week 1 (rho = -0.85, p = 0.019), but neither met the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold (α = 0.010). SpO2 increased across the camp, with week 3 significantly higher than weeks 1 and 2 after Bonferroni correction, whereas RHR was significantly lower in week 3 than in week 1, but not week 2, after correction. Athlete-reported outcomes remained stable, acute mountain sickness symptoms were minimal, and haematological and iron-status markers showed no significant pre-to-post changes. Sleep difficulty showed a transient descriptive increase during the initial phase of the altitude camp, while SpO2 and RHR changes were consistent with physiological acclimatisation. Chronotype-related differences in sleep difficulty appeared to be present before altitude exposure rather than emerging specifically during the camp. Given the small sample size, these findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

title: Limb Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in Rats is partially mediated by enhancing Necroptosis via Phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL.
abstract: Limb ischemia-reperfusion injury (L-IRI) causes severe skeletal muscle damage and functional impairment through activation of regulated cell-death and inflammatory pathways. Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrotic cell death mediated through the receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-RIPK3-mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) signaling axis. Prior experimental studies have shown that Necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) attenuates acute skeletal muscle ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. However, how Nec-1-sensitive protection relates to RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, circulating muscle injury markers, inflammatory responses, histological damage, and functional recovery during the early postischemic period remains incompletely defined. In this study, we used a rat model of unilateral hindlimb ischemia involving 3 hours of ischemia followed by reperfusion for up to 7 days to evaluate these interrelated responses. Nec-1 was administered before ischemia and after reperfusion. L-IRI resulted in elevated plasma creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels, severe histopathological injury, increased TUNEL staining, impaired grip strength, and reduced Modified Tarlov scores. These changes were accompanied by increased phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL, activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, and altered expression of injury-associated inflammatory mediators. Nec-1 treatment reduced RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, inflammatory mediator expression, circulating muscle injury markers, and histological injury while preserving muscle architecture and improving functional recovery. These findings support and extend previous evidence that Nec-1-sensitive necroptosis-associated signaling contributes to early skeletal muscle injury following L-IRI. Pharmacologic targeting of regulated necrotic and inflammatory pathways warrants further investigation as a potential adjunct strategy for limiting acute skeletal muscle injury after limb reperfusion.

title: Mechanobiology in Osteoarthritis: From Crosstalk of Mechanosensitive Signaling Pathways to the Intervention Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential of Exercise.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most prevalent joint degeneration globally. Once considered passive "wear and tear", it is now recognized as a metabolically active, whole-joint disease driven by genetic, metabolic, inflammatory, and mechanical factors. The core pathology is failed mechanotransduction, where a dysregulated mechanosensitive signaling network disrupts joint homeostasis, causing cartilage degradation, synovitis, and pain. This review re-examines OA pathogenesis through network biology, highlighting that OA stems from the dysregulation of a complex mechanosensitive network-including Piezo, Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 4 (TRPV4), Integrin-Focal Adhesion Kinase (integrin-FAK), Hippo/yes-associated protein-transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (Hippo/YAP-TAZ), and Wingless/Integrated /β-catenin (Wnt/β-catenin) pathways. These pathways engage in extensive crosstalk via shared secondary messengers (calcium ions, reactive oxygen species) to determine cell fate. Furthermore, exercise acts as a physiological "mechanotherapy" to recalibrate this network, shifting cellular responses from catabolic/inflammatory states to anabolic/homeostatic ones. We also explore the translational potential of restoring network balance using precision mechanotherapy, advanced drug delivery, and biomaterials. OA is fundamentally a systemic network failure from failed mechanotransduction. Future therapies should shift from single-target interventions to systemic reprogramming of the dysregulated network. Utilizing biomaterials, smart drug delivery, and personalized exercise can advance OA management from symptomatic relief to active tissue regeneration and disease reversal.

title: Are both hemolysis and impaired myocyte integrity associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
abstract: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is a potent antioxidant enzyme. G6PD deficiency, predominant among males, is a neonatal "neurotoxic" risk, characterized by episodic hemolysis that is sometimes infection triggered. Clinical risk among heterozygous G6PD-deficient females is often under-recognized. Recent reports of rhabdomyolysis among G6PD-deficient individuals are reviewed here. In one case, a male athlete with G6PD deficiency (<10% activity) experienced multiple, acute episodes of rhabdomyolysis, painful muscle symptomatology, injury and hemolysis after strenuous exertion. Both his mother with G6PD-deficiency (<45% activity) and maternal grandmother have chronic histories of episodic or triggered fatigue-related disruptive symptoms. Other case reports of G6PD-deficient individuals with muscle injury and exertional symptoms (with or without hemolysis) showed unique laboratory findings of elevated creatine kinase, myoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, and aminotransferases levels and myoglobinuria. Disrupted myocyte energetics and loss of cellular integrity can be attributed to impaired downstream pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)-related oxidant stress protection, which is a key enzymatic consequence of G6PD-deficiency. These triggered stresses may explain the muscle fatigue and propensity to exertional injury. Correlation between stress-sensitive-impaired muscle injury among all G6PD-deficient individuals, including neonates, requires further clinical validation to ascertain oxidant-stress impact of impaired PPP-dependent cellular energetics of red blood, white blood, neural, and muscle cells.

title: Beware the Muscle: Silent Exercise-Induced Aminotransferase Elevation as a Diagnostic Pitfall in Hepatology and Pretreatment Screening-A Report of Two Cases.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In clinical hepatology practice, pretreatment liver enzyme screening plays a key role in making management decisions, such as initiation of antituberculosis therapy or surveillance of chronic hepatitis B. Unrecognized extrahepatic sources of aminotransferase elevations can lead to misdiagnosis, inappropriate treatment alteration, and unnecessary invasive or costly investigations.
CASE PRESENTATION: We present two cases of active young males who were undergoing liver biochemical testing for therapeutic decision-making for other underlying illnesses. Patient one was undergoing baseline liver enzyme testing prior to first-line antituberculosis treatment initiation while patient two was undergoing surveillance for e-antigen-negative hepatitis B infection. Both patients had asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations mimicking acute hepatocellular injury. There was a marked and disproportionate elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) relative to alanine aminotransferase (ALT), in the setting of otherwise normal cholestatic and synthetic parameters. Targeted history revealed heavy resistance weight training prior to testing. Measurement of serum creatine kinase (CK) confirmed exercise-induced muscle injury, demonstrating elevated CK concentrations that paralleled the AST trajectory. Cessation of strenuous training led to rapid normalization of aminotransferases and a decline in CK levels, without interruption of tuberculosis management or unwarranted antiviral initiation.
CONCLUSION: Clinically silent exertional muscle injury is an underappreciated mimicker of acute liver injury. In patients presenting with isolated or disproportionate AST elevation, confirming a myogenic enzyme source via CK quantification can prevent misdiagnosis, eliminate unnecessary liver-directed workup, and avoid inappropriate modification or initiation of essential pharmacotherapy.

title: Supporting adolescent menstrual health to improve participation and performance in physical activity: rapid realist review to inform a logic model for intervention development.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insufficient physical activity is higher in women and girls globally, with increased risk of non-communicable diseases. Menstrual (period-related) symptoms are a recognised barrier to adolescents engaging in physical activity. There is a lack of evidence-based guidance to address this barrier.
OBJECTIVE: To develop a set of initial programme theories (context-mechanism-outcome configurations, CMOCs) to describe how existing menstrual health support interventions work, for whom, how and in what circumstances to inform a logic model for intervention development.
DESIGN: Rapid realist review.
METHODS: Formal, double-screened, database (Medline, AMED, Embase, Psycinfo, CINAHL, ERIC, SCOPUS; June 2025) and grey literature searches guided by stakeholder expertise. Articles were selected that met inclusion criteria and contributed to theory development. Explanatory statements were extracted and synthesised into CMOCs using Pawson’s reasoning processes and mapped onto Self-Determination Theory concepts (autonomy, competency, relatedness).
RESULTS: From 9585 database hits, 63 articles were included. Three generated initial programme theories describe how four identified intervention domains (education; practicalities including toilet facilities, clothing and free accessible period products; menstrual cycle tracking and screening tools; and medical support if needed) could improve menstrual health confidence and understanding (M), communication and trust (M)—to empower individuals to enhance their own menstrual health (M) and potentially improve participation rates and performance in physical activity (O). Alternative causal pathways describe potential adverse outcomes when processes are not in place to: signpost to medical support if needed (M), support user trust in how and why data are collected and used (M) and enable understanding of the limitations of menstrual health support tools (M). Contextual data are needed to further refine these theories that are presented as a logic model.
CONCLUSION: The proposed logic model can be used to inform and evaluate future interventions aimed at overcoming menstrual health related barriers with physical activity.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD420251066742.

title: Young Investigator Award: Where Do We Start? A Conceptual Model for Implementing Menstrual Cycle Tracking in Sport.
abstract: Menstrual cycle tracking is a much-discussed component of the ' female athlete' research theme; however, more translational work is needed to meet practitioners' desire for further guidance on the implementation of tracking in applied settings. The purpose of this paper is to present a preliminary conceptual model to inform practitioners' decision-making around menstrual cycle tracking and assist researchers in identifying and framing future research directions. The proposed model-Conducting and Navigating menstrual cycle Education, Communication and Tracking (ConNECT)-proposes that communication and education strategies may be utilised to affect social, organisational and individual level change, ultimately supporting the implementation of menstrual cycle tracking by increasing its uptake and impact. This model was developed based on the findings from a series of studies conducted by the authors, which considered the existing literature on tracking and the perspectives of athletes and practitioners. Therefore, the ConNECT model offers an ecologically sound starting point for sport scientists, coaches and other members of an athlete's support team to base their practice on.

title: Varying Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Femoral Fixation Points and Fixation Flexion Angles Do Not Affect ACL Graft Force and Tibiofemoral Motion After ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The addition of lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) to anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR) has been shown to reduce rotational laxity and improve graft survivorship. Despite the increased utilization of LET with ACLR, there remains a lack of consensus on the ideal location of the femoral attachment site of LET.
PURPOSE: To compare ACL graft force and tibiofemoral motion in cadaveric specimens undergoing ACLR with the addition of LET at varying fixation angles and fixation points.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees were tested in 6 conditions, including LET fixation at 2 anatomic locations. Location 1 was defined as 8 mm proximal and 4 to 5 mm posterior to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the anterolateral ligament. Location 2 was defined as 31 mm proximal to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the distal Kaplan fibers. The testing conditions were as follows: (1) native; (2) ACLR; (3) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 30°; (4) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 30°; (5) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 60°; and (6) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 60°. Specimens were mounted on a 6 degrees of freedom robotic system to assess tibial internal rotation and anterior tibial translation at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90° of knee flexion. A load cell was utilized to assess ACL graft force.
RESULTS: There were no differences between the 4 LET states in any outcome. In internal rotation, the addition of LET demonstrated reductions in ACL graft force in all 4 configurations, ranging from -14.9 N (14%) to -19.5 N (20%) at 0°, -19.7 N (51%) to -21.4 N (55%) at 30°, and -3.9 N (30%) to -4.6 N (35%) at 60° (all P < .05). The addition of LET also demonstrated reductions in internal rotation range of motion in all 4 configurations, ranging from -1.86° (15%) to -2.45° (19%) at 0°, -4.87° (18%) to -5.75° (20%) at 30°, and -4.70° (19%) to -5.92° (23%) at 60° (all P < .05).
CONCLUSION: Variations in LET fixation location and fixation flexion angle did not alter its effect on ACL graft force reduction or tibiofemoral motion in the cadaveric knee. The addition of LET had a protective effect on the ACL graft in internal rotation while demonstrating overconstraint compared to the native knee.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings suggest that surgeons may have flexibility in selecting the femoral fixation location and knee flexion angle for LET without substantially altering its biomechanical effect on ACL graft loading or tibiofemoral kinematics. However, because LET reduced internal rotation beyond the native state, care should be taken to avoid excessive constraint when performing the procedure.

title: Evaluation of a four-herb Chinese medicine formula at different concentrations on muscle damage and inflammation in a rat model of DOMS.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) impairs exercise recovery, while current treatments remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) formulas may provide safe, multi-target interventions.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the dose-dependent protective effects of a four-herb Chinese medicine formulation (safflower, Chinese Angelica, peach kernel and myrrh) against DOMS in a rat model.
METHODS: Thirty-two male SPF SD rats were randomly allocated to control or low- (1696 mg/kg), medium- (3392 mg/kg), or high-dose (6784 mg/kg) groups. The formulation was administered orally for 11 days, with DOMS induced by exhaustive swimming on day 8. Serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-exercise.
RESULTS: The medium- and high-dose groups exhibited significantly lower serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 levels than controls, with the high-dose group showing the largest reductions. The low-dose group showed limited or no significant reductions in most markers, demonstrating a clear dose-dependent protective effect.
CONCLUSIONS: The formulation dose-dependently attenuates muscle damage and inflammation in a rat DOMS model, with high-dose treatment achieving the fastest recovery. Clinical trials are warranted to confirm the efficacy and safety in humans.

title: Integration of dynamic apnea into routine coach-led training in competitive BMX riders: A controlled pilot study.
abstract: Dynamic apnea (DA) has been proposed as a conditioning strategy for high-intensity exercise, but its integration into routine BMX training has not been investigated. We examined the effects of an eight-week DA program integrated into coach-led BMX training. Nineteen competitive BMX riders entered the study; 12 completed the protocol (AG, n = 6; CG, n = 6). AG performed repeated apneas during selected cycling sections, while CG completed matched training without apnea. Sprint performance, heart-rate responses, maximal static apnea and post-exercise blood lactate were assessed before and after training. AG improved 300-m performance compared with CG (adjusted difference: -0.79 s; p = 0.017), whereas no significant between-group differences were observed for 500-m and start performance. Peak heart rate was lower in AG than CG after training during the 300-m and 500-m performances. Maximal static apnea increased, with a stronger and faster bradycardic response in AG than CG. Blood lactate did not differ significantly between groups, although four of six AG riders showed a marked reduction. Among protocol completers, DA was integrated into supervised routine BMX training and was associated with improved 300-m performance and cardiovascular adaptations. These preliminary findings require confirmation in larger cohorts.

title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.

title: M4-like Macrophages Drive Skeletal Muscle Fibrosis and Suppress Myogenesis via the MMP12/SPP1/NF-κB Axis.
abstract: Acute skeletal muscle repair depends on a finely tuned balance between myogenic regeneration and fibrotic remodeling. Macrophages are essential to this process, and specific subsets have been linked to fibrosis in some organs. The M4-like macrophage, a distinct polarization subset implicated in fibrotic diseases, has not been well characterized in the context of injured muscle, particularly regarding its impact on fibroblast activation and myogenic suppression. The study aims to explore the effects of M4-like macrophages in the repair of muscle injury and possible mechanism. We analyzed a murine single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset from cardiotoxin (CTX)-injured skeletal muscle to identify injury-expanded macrophage subsets and their molecular programs. Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining of muscle sections were used to assess CXCL4 expression and platelet (CD41+) infiltration in injured versus uninjured tissues. CXCL4-induced M4-like macrophages were established as an in vitro model to examine their effects on L929 fibroblasts and C2C12 myoblasts. The MMP12-SPP1 interaction was predicted by AlphaFold3 and validated by co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence colocalization. Loss-of-function and rescue experiments targeting MMP12 and SPP1 were performed to determine their causal roles in fibroblast activation and myogenic suppression. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses were used to define downstream macrophage-intrinsic NF-κB/TNF-α signaling. Finally, AAV-mediated macrophage-targeted SPP1 knockdown and pharmacological NF-κB inhibition were evaluated in the CTX injury model. Using a BALB/c mouse model of cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced acute skeletal muscle injury and a publicly available murine scRNA-seq dataset from CTX-injured skeletal muscle, we observed an injury-induced MMP12/SPP1-positive macrophage subset with an M4-like transcriptional signature. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation assays and immunofluorescence colocalization supported an association between MMP12 and SPP1. MMP12 knockdown attenuated the pro-fibrotic and anti-myogenic effects of M4-like macrophages, whereas recombinant SPP1 largely restored these phenotypes. Furthermore, transcriptomic and biochemical analyses revealed that autocrine SPP1 activated NF-κB signaling in M4-like macrophages, and increased TNF-α secretion. Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB signaling with QNZ reduced fibroblast activation and restored the expression of myogenic markers. However, QNZ is not TNF-α specific and may affect multiple cell types. In vivo, AAV-mediated macrophage-targeted SPP1 knockdown driven by the F4/80 promoter, as well as QNZ treatment in the CTX-induced muscle injury model, markedly decreased collagen deposition, enhanced myogenic regeneration, and improved functional recovery. These findings identify an MMP12/SPP1/NF-κB signaling pathway in M4-like macrophages, with TNF-α as a potential downstream mediator, that may contribute to an imbalance between regeneration and fibrosis and may represent a therapeutic target for enhancing skeletal muscle repair after acute injury.
