title: Role of integrin αvβ5 receptor and microglia in delayed-onset muscle soreness in mice.
abstract: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is characterized by muscle pain, stiffness, and tenderness following intense or unaccustomed exercise. In humans, symptoms typically arise 6-72 h post-exercise. This study investigated a novel mechanism underlying DOMS, focusing on the involvement of the irisin receptor integrin αvβ5 and spinal microglia in its development. Male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to a DOMS model induced by an acute aerobic exercise protocol, and nociceptive thresholds were assessed using the von Frey filament test. The role of spinal integrin αvβ5 was evaluated via intrathecal administration of the antagonist cilengitide, given both prior to exercise and 24 h post-exercise. To assess irisin's nociceptive effects, it was also administered intrathecally. Additionally, minocycline, a microglial inhibitor, was administered before irisin to determine microglial involvement. An in vitro assay evaluated microglial activation by irisin via flow cytometry. Pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines were quantified by ELISA. Cilengitide reversed exercise-induced DOMS and reduced spinal pro-inflammatory cytokines. Irisin induced nociception, which was attenuated by minocycline. Irisin also activated microglia in vitro, increasing pro-inflammatory cytokine production. These findings suggest integrin αvβ5 and spinal microglia play critical roles in DOMS pathogenesis, with irisin and pro-inflammatory cytokines as key mediators.

title: Binding of a Novel 11β-Hydroxysteroid to the Apelin Receptor (APLNR) and Its Possible Role in Regulating Skeletal Muscle Health in Mice.
abstract: Several molecules have been investigated for their potential to improve muscle health in models of muscle damage simulating sarcopenia, injury, or aging. Some small molecules induced beneficial effects on skeletal muscle by stimulating the apelin receptor (APLNR). This receptor has emerged as a promising pharmacological target for modulating muscle homeostasis. Using an in silico approach, we recently identified 11β-hydroxypregnenolone (11β-OHP5) as a potential skeletal muscle (SKM) modulator. We hypothesized that 11β-OHP5 interacts with and activates APLNR. This study employed several research approaches: (1) in silico molecular docking and molecular dynamics to explore the feasibility of 11β-OHP5 interacting with APLNR; (2) in vitro activation analysis to APLNR; (3) in vitro analysis C2C12 myoblast differentiation; (4) analysis of the molecule's presence in mouse skeletal muscle and its differential presence between young and older mice. The results show that 11β-OHP5, acting through APLNR, positively affects myoblast differentiation and may participate in the exercise-induced benefits in aging mice. We show that 11β-OHP5 interacts with APLNR, induces myogenic responses, is found in SKM; its concentration decreases with age, and exercise restores it. More work is necessary to understand the physiology of this possible endogenous molecule.

title: Aerobic Exercise Ameliorates Osteoarthritic Chondrocyte Degradation in Osteoarthritis via Regulating E2F8/NLRP14 Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Although physical activity is known to mitigate disease risks, its protective molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. E2F8, a regulator of cell cycle and metabolism, showed significant differential expression between osteoarthritis (OA) and exercise models, suggesting it may link mechanical activity to OA alleviation. In vitro, Interleukin-1 Beta (IL-1β) simulated inflammation. In vivo, OA was induced in rats via Monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection. The effects of E2F8 and mechanical stress were assessed using moderate treadmill exercise, histology, and joint observation. Bioinformatic analysis, cyclic tensile strain, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and gene knockdown were used to investigate mechanisms. In OA rats, E2F8 was downregulated in cartilage while NLRP14 increased. Exercise reversed E2F8 downregulation, alleviated cartilage degeneration, restored anabolic activity, and reduced inflammatory catabolism linked to senescence. In vitro, mechanical stress reversed the IL-1β-induced anabolic/catabolic imbalance by regulating the E2F8/NLRP14, mitigating OA progression. Mechanical stress enhances E2F8 expression in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, which in turn protects cartilage by suppressing the expression of NLRP14. These findings underscore the role of E2F8 as a mechano-sensitive mediator and highlight the potential of exercise or exercise-mimetic therapies as effective strategies for preventing and treating OA.
